title: Introduction
intro: Macroeconomics is defined as that branch of economics which studies economic issues or economic problems at the level of an economy as a whole.

lessons.title: Meaning, origin and principal concerns
lessons.body: Macroeconomics is defined as that branch of economics which studies economic issues or economic problems at the level of an economy as a whole. The term Macro comes from Makros, meaning large. Keynes’ The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) established macroeconomics as a separate branch. Its principal concerns are employment, inflation, growth of output and depression. Keynes stressed government intervention when inadequate demand reduces output and employment.

lessons.title: Microeconomics versus macroeconomics
lessons.body: Microeconomics studies scarcity and choice at the level of an individual, household, firm or industry; allocation of resources is its central issue. Macroeconomics studies these problems for the economy as a whole; determination of overall output and employment is its central issue. Micro uses partial equilibrium analysis, studying one market while holding other markets constant. Macro uses general equilibrium analysis, examining simultaneous equilibrium across markets. An industry is an aggregate, but studying one industry is still microeconomics.

lessons.title: Micro–macro paradox and interdependence
lessons.body: What is logical at the micro level may not be logical at the macro level. Saving may improve one person’s future prosperity; if everyone saves more by spending less, aggregate demand, investment, output and employment may fall. Macro affects micro when an RBI interest-rate change affects one producer’s borrowing. Micro affects macro when individual increases in spending together raise aggregate demand.

lessons.title: Scope and significance
lessons.body: Macroeconomics studies national income, employment, general prices, growth, money, banking, government budgets and international transactions. It helps explain an economy’s functioning and formulate policies for growth with stability. Keep the level of analysis clear: the price of one product is micro; the general price level is macro.

1.1 ABOUT MACROECONOMICS
• Origin of the Term: The term Macro in English has its origin in the Greek term Makros which
means Large. In the context of macroeconomics, 'large' means economy as a whole.
• Emergence of Macroeconomics
• Macroeconomics emerged as a separate branch of economics in 1936 with the publication of
a celebrated book titled "The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money" by John
Maynard Keynes.
• The book emphasised the role of the government when the economy is in a state of depression
(when the level of output and employment tends to fall owing to lack of demand in the economy).
• Keynes discarded the long-held belief that the market forces of supply and demand would
automatically tackle the problem of unemployment and low level of output.
• Meaning of Macroeconomics: Macroeconomics is defined as that branch of economics which
studies economic issues or economic problems at the level of an economy as a whole.

Introductory Macroeconomics
• Principal Concerns of Macroeconomics
• Employment for the residents,
• The problem of price rise (inflation),
• Growth of output in the economy,
• The problem of depression.

MICROECONOMICS vs. MACROECONOMICS
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Micro-Macro Paradox
What is logical at the micro level may not be logical at the macro level.
Illustration
Saving - A virtue at micro level
• If an individual saves more, he adds to his future prosperity. This makes saving a virtue at micro level.
Saving -A vice at macro level
• If all the people in an economy save more (and spend less), demand for goods and services may
decline. Consequently, investment may decline; production and employment level may fall.
• The economy will be driven towards future poverty rather than prosperity. This makes saving a vice at
the macro level.
Micro-Macro Interdependence
• Macro impacts Micro: For instance, increase in interest rate by the RBI (and consequently by the
commercial banks) will lower borrowings for investment by the individual producers.
• Micro impacts Macro: For instance, increase in spending at the individual level (which is a
microeconomic factor) will lead to a rise in AD (aggregate demand) in the economy (which is a
macroeconomic factor). Increase in AD induces higher investment, leading to a rise in the level of
output and employment in the economy (again the macroeconomic factors).
AVLR 1.2

CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Q. 1. Distinguish between partial equilibrium and general equilibrium.
Ans.
(i) Partial equilibrium refers to equilibrium in one market (say, commodity market) on the
assumption that there is no change in other markets (like labour market or capital market).
It is the method of study in microeconomics.
(ii) General equilibrium refers to simultaneous equilibrium in all the markets in the economy.
It is the method of study in macroeconomics.

1.3.2 Significance of Macroeconomics
The following observations highlight the significance of macroeconomics:
(1) Description of the Economy: Macroeconomics offers a deep description of the economy.
Here are some key elements it covers and their associated benefits.
• Estimation of national income (across different sectors) reveals the nature and level of
economic activity in the economy.
• Study of unemployment reveals the extent of the problem and the way it can be handled.
• Government budget reveals the way economy is regulated by the government.
(2) Roadmap for Business Decisions: Description of the economy serves as a roadmap for
business decisions.
Example:
Rising national income (and consequently rising consumer expenditure) over time will
induce the business houses to expand their investment, leading to expansion of output
and employment.
(3) Policy Formulation: Macroeconomic data helps in formulation of government policies.
Example:
Data on 'people below poverty line' will facilitate an appropriate policy relating to DBT
(direct benefit transfer) for poorer sections of the society.
(4) Global Economic Issues: Study of macroeconomics brings to the fore the global economic
issues such as 'exchange rate' in the international money market, and movement of FDI
(Foreign Direct Investment) across different countries of the world.
(5) Environmental Pollution and Sustainable Development: It is through macroeconomic
analysis that we can approach the issues related to environmental pollution, and formulate a
strategy of sustainable development
(6) Structural Changes and Growth Path of the Economy: Study of macroeconomics helps
understand structural changes in the economy. Changes in occupational structure of a
country, for example, is an important macroeconomic information that helps trace the
nature and pace of economic growth over time.

Emergence of Macroeconomics as a Separate Branch of Economics
• Great Depression of 1930's is a landmark event that led to the emergence of macroeconomics as a
separate branch of economics. It does not mean that the concept of macroeconomics did not exist
prior to this event. But, macroeconomics (prior to the Great Depression) was considered more like
an extension of microeconomics: it did not exist as a separate (or specialised) branch of economics.
Of course, there was a reason to it:
• It was a long-held belief of the classical economists (economists prior to Keynes) that the principles of
microeconomics were enough to explain the behaviour of the economy as a whole. The argument runs
like this:
• Microeconomics teaches us that (in pursuit of self-interest) every individual (in a market economy
or a free economy maximises his satisfaction with his given income.
• Maximisation of individual satisfaction (or welfare) implies the maximisation of welfare of all the
individuals in the economy. It implies maximisation of social welfare.
• If social welfare is maximised, the scarce resources in the economy must have been optimally
utilised.
• Microeconomics further teaches us that in a free economy (or under perfect competition), all
markets tend to be in a state of equilibrium. Thus, in the labour market S_= D (supply of labour
= demand for labour). It is a situation of full employment.
• There could be unemployment when S, > DL. But, in such a situation wage rate would fall, leading
to a fall in S, and rise in Dy. Eventually, the situation of full employment would automatically be
restored. Thus, full employment is a normal feature of a market economy.
• Briefly, the principles of microeconomics explain that in a free economy:
(i) social welfare is maximised,
(i) resources are optimally utilised, and
(i) full employment is a normal situation.
• Accordingly, the classical economists concluded that the principles of microeconomics were enough
to explain the behaviour of the economic activity at the macro level. There was no need to consider
macroeconomics as a separate branch of economics.
Great Depression of 1930's contradicted the Classical Thought
• During the depression of 30's, economic events unfolded in such a manner that the classical thought
was totally contradicted. Following points are of notable significance in this regard:
() The depression of 30's led to huge unemployment in the developed countries of the world (North
America and Europe.
(i) In USA, unemployment shot up from 3% to 25% between the period 1929-33.
(i lie mployment was accompanied with a fall in GDP, Between the period 1929-33, GDP in USA fell
by about 33%.
Introduction
(iv) Fall in GDP led to a fall in AD (aggregate demand). Accordingly, there were drastic cuts in output as
planned by the producers across all sectors of the economy.
(v) Cut in planned output implied a further fall in employment and GDP in the economy.
• Thus, during the depression of 30's, the western economies were driven into the vicious circle of low
demand and low GDP. This circle operated as under:
Low AD → Low planned output Low level of employment → Low GDP → Low AD
• This is called 'Low Level Equilibrium Trap'.
• The classical economists failed to find any answer to this low level equilibrium trap. Market forces
of supply and demand failed to break it. It is in such a situation that macroeconomics emerged as a
separate branch of economics. Prof. Keynes was the pioneer in the field of modern macroeconomics.
He invented several macroeconomic variables (like AD and AS) and formulated a macroeconomic model
to break the vicious circle of 'low level equilibrium trap'. He diagnosed lack of AD as the root cause of the
problem, and suggested large scale expenditure by the government as a remedy.

issues) at the level of an economy as a whole.
• Macroeconomics as different from Microeconomics
• Microeconomics deals with the problem of choice and scarcity at the individual level, while
macroeconomics does it at the level of an economy as a whole.
• Allocation of resources is the central issue in microeconomics, while in macroeconomics the
central issue is the determination of national income and employment.
• Microeconomics uses microeconomic variables (like consumer's demand and producer's supply),
while macroeconomics uses macroeconomic variables (like AD and AS).
• Microeconomics involves lesser degree of aggregation than macroeconomics.
• Microeconomics and macroeconomics are based on different set of assumptions.
• Scope and Significance of Macroeconomics

(ii) Theory of employment
(iii) Theory of money

(vi) Exchange rate and balance of payments

(ii) Macroeconomic data serves as a roadmap for business decisions.
(iii) Macroeconomic data facilitates policy formulation by the government.
(iv) Macroeconomics helps understand global economic issues.
(v) Macroeconomics underlines the gravity of environmental

title: Some Basic Concepts of Macroeconomics
intro: Final goods are those goods which have crossed the boundary line of production and are ready for use by their final users.

lessons.title: Final goods, intermediate goods and end use
lessons.body: Final goods are those goods which have crossed the boundary line of production and are ready for use by their final users. They lead to final consumption expenditure or investment expenditure. Intermediate goods are purchased by one firm from another for resale or for use as raw material in producing other goods. Classification depends on end use, not the physical nature of the good: milk bought by a household is final; milk bought by an ice-cream producer is intermediate. Unsold additions to inventory count as investment.
lessons.textbookHeading: 2.1 MEANING OF END-USE CLASSIFICATION OF GOODS

lessons.title: Consumption goods versus capital goods
lessons.body: Consumption goods directly satisfy human wants. They include durable goods, non-durable goods, semi-durable goods and services. Capital goods are fixed assets of producers, repeatedly used in production: durable-use producer goods such as plant and machinery. A household car is a durable consumption good; a taxi used to produce transport services is a capital good. Both are final goods. A capital good is not intermediate merely because it helps produce something.
lessons.textbookHeading: 2.1.1 Final Goods · Consumption Goods · Capital Goods

lessons.title: Consumption expenditure and investment
lessons.body: Consumption expenditure includes expenditure by households, government and non-profit private institutions. Investment is a process of adding to the stock of capital. Fixed investment adds to fixed assets; inventory investment changes stocks of raw materials, semi-finished goods and finished goods. New residential construction is investment. Buying existing shares transfers financial ownership; it does not itself create new capital goods. Inventory investment can be negative when closing stock is less than opening stock.
lessons.formula:
Inventory investment = Closing stock − Opening stock
Gross investment = Fixed investment + Inventory investment

lessons.title: Gross investment, net investment and depreciation
lessons.body: Net investment refers to the increase in the stock of capital during an accounting year. Gross investment includes replacement of worn-out capital. Depreciation, also called consumption of fixed capital, refers to loss of value of fixed assets in use through normal wear and tear, normal accidental damage and expected obsolescence. Unexpected destruction is a capital loss rather than normal depreciation. A depreciation reserve fund is kept to cope with depreciation losses.
lessons.formula:
Net investment = Gross investment − Depreciation
Depreciation per year = (Capital value − Scrap value) ÷ Estimated life
lessons.textbookHeading: 2.3.3 Gross Investment, Net Investment and the Concept of Depreciation

lessons.title: Stocks and flows
lessons.body: Stocks are quantities measured at a point of time; flows are quantities measured over a specified period of time. Wealth, money supply, capital and bank balances are stocks. Income, consumption, investment and saving are flows. Capital is a stock; investment is the flow adding to it. “Money supply on 31 March” is a stock even though money changes hands repeatedly.

lessons.title: Four sectors and circular flow of income
lessons.body: The household sector supplies factor services and consumes goods. The producing sector produces goods and services. Government acts as a welfare agency and producer; the external sector links the domestic economy with the rest of the world. Real flows are flows of goods and factor services; money flows are payments and receipts in the opposite direction. Circular flow of income refers to the circularity of production, income and expenditure across sectors. In a simple two-sector model, production generates income and income generates expenditure.
lessons.formula:
Production → Income generation → Expenditure → Production
Value of output = Factor income = Final expenditure
lessons.textbookHeading: 2.5 FOUR SECTORS · 2.6 INTERSECTORAL FLOWS · 2.7 CIRCULAR FLOW OF INCOME

lessons.title: Types of consumption goods
lessons.body: Durable-use consumer goods serve consumers repeatedly over a long period, such as cars and refrigerators. Semi-durable goods serve over a shorter period, such as clothes. Non-durable goods are used up in a single act of consumption, such as food. Services are intangible acts satisfying wants, such as teaching or medical treatment. Durability alone does not make an item a capital good: capital goods are used by producers in production.

lessons.title: Why final goods are counted and intermediate goods are not
lessons.textbookHeading: ABILITY ZONE · Significance of the Distinction between Intermediate Goods and Final Goods
lessons.body: Intermediate inputs are embodied in final output. Counting both adds the same value more than once. If cloth worth ₹5,000 becomes shirts worth ₹7,000, final output is ₹7,000, not ₹12,000. Under the value-added method, the cloth producer’s value and the shirt producer’s additional ₹2,000 are each counted once. It is incorrect to say intermediate goods contribute nothing: their contribution is included in final value.

• In economics, a good which has crossed the boundary line of production and is ready for use by

• On the other hand, a good which has not crossed the boundary line of production and is not ready

- As used by the producers, 50 tonnes of paper will be considered as Intermediate Good.
(Because ithas not reached its final users and is yet to cross the boundary line of production).

CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
End-use Classification of Goods
• End-use classification of goods is that classification which classifies goods on the basis of their
end-use and end-users, rather than their physical characteristics.
- Goods are classified as 'Final Goods' when goods have crossed the boundary line of production, and
are ready for use by their final users.
- Goods are classified as 'Intermediate Goods' when goods are within the boundary line of production
and are not ready for use by their final users.
- Good are classified as 'Consumer Goods' when goods are used for the direct satisfaction of households.
- Goods are classified as 'Capital Goods' when goods are used as fixed assets by the producers.

2.1.1 Final Goods
• Final goods are those goods which have crossed the boundary line of production and are ready
for use by their final users.
• Who are the final users?
• These are (i) consumers, and (i) producers.
• How are Final Goods classified?
• Final goods are classified as: (i) final consumer goods, and (ii) final producer goods.
(i) Final consumer goods are finally purchased by the consumers for the satisfaction of
their wants.
(ii) Final producer goods are finally purchased by the producers and are generally used as
fixed assets in the process of production.

What do we mean when we say that final goods have crossed the boundary line of production?
• We mean that these goods are out of the process of production or the process of value addition,
and have reached their final users.
A shirt in a retail showroom is all set for sale to its final user. No value is to be added to the
shirt by way of stitching, ironing, packaging, etc.
Is it to be treated as a final good?
"No' should be the answer. Because:
The final stage of value addition occurs only when the shirt is finally sold to the consumer
(the final user), If the retailer buys the shirt for & 800 and sells to the consumer for 7 1,000,
there is value addition of & 200.
To repeat, the value addition process is completed only when the product reaches its final
user: it may be a shirt purchased by the consumer, or a tractor purchased by a farmer (Both,
the consumer and the farmer are the final users).
• You may note that only final goods are included in the estimation of national product or
national income.
2.1.1 (a) Consumption Goods or Consumer Goods
• Consumption goods (or consumer goods) are those goods which are directly used for the
satisfaction of human wants.
Example:
Ice cream and milk as used by the households. These goods are consumed by the households
when purchased.

2.1.1 (b) Capital Goods
• Capital goods are fixed assets of the producers. Plant and machinery is an example of capital
goods. As fixed assets, capital goods are repeatedly used in the process of production for several
years and are of high value. Even nuts and bolts are used for several years, but these are not
capital goods as these are of low value. Only those fixed assets of the producers are taken as
capital goods which are used in the process of production for several years and which are of
high value.
• Also, capital goods involve depreciation. Depreciation refers to loss of value of fixed assets (in
use) owing to their wear and tear.
• These goods are used by the producers either for:
(i) the replacement of the existing capital stock, or for
(ii) addition to the capital stock.
DID YOU KNOW
All Machines are not Capital Goods, for example:
• A sewing machine in a tailoring shop is a fixed asset of the tailor; it is a capital good.
• But the same machine with a consumer household is not a capital good. It is simply a durable-use
consumer good.
• Likewise, a car with a tourist company is a capital good. But the same car with a household is a
durable-use consumer good.
• Thus, while identifying goods as capital goods, we must make sure about their end-user.
- If the end-user of a durable good is a household consumer, it is durable-use consumer good.
- On the other hand, if the end-user of a durable good is a producer, it is a capital good.
Finally, capital goods are only those durable goods which are used as producer goods, not as
consumer goods.

2.1.2 Intermediate Goods
• Intermediate goods are those goods
(i) which have yet not crossed the boundary line of production,
(ii) value is still to be added to these goods, and
(iii) which are yet not ready for use by their final users.
• In other words, intermediate goods are those goods which are purchased by one firm from the
other firm: (i) as raw material, or (ii) as goods for resale.
Example:
(i) Wood purchased by a carpenter (from a timber merchant) for making chairs is an
intermediate good. Because, wood is used as a raw material for making chairs. Value is
to be added to wood by converting it into chairs.
(ii) Shirts purchased by firm X from firm Y for resale are intermediate goods. Because, value
is to be added to the shirts through resale.
• Non-inclusion in National Income: Value of intermediate goods ultimately becomes a part of the
value of final goods.
• Accordingly, intermediate goods are not included in the
estimation of national product or
national income.
• Otherwise, there would be duplication in the estimation of national product, called 'Double
Counting' (counting the value of a good more than once).
Example:
When a carpenter buys wood worth 10,000 and converts it into chairs worth & 20,000,
then the value of chairs (final goods) includes the value of wood (intermediate good). If we
add R 10,000 (wood) + R 20,000 (chairs), the total becomes & 30,000. Thus, leading to double
counting ofF 10,000.
• Expenditure on Intermediate Goods: Expenditure on intermediate goods by the producers
during an accounting year is called intermediate consumption or intermediate cost.
Same Good May be Final or Intermediate
• It is not possible to name one set of goods as final goods and another set as intermediate goods.
The same good may be final or intermediate good. The distinction depends on the end-use of the
goods.

Ans. Expenditure on final goods must lead to:

Q. 4. Purchase of a car always means the purchase of a final good. Do you agree?
Ans. No. It depends on the end-use of the car. If it is purchased by a household, it is a final good. It is
like a consumer durable.
If it is purchased by taxi-operators, then again it is a final good, as it is to be finally used by the
producer as a fixed asset.
However, if the car is purchased by a retail dealer from the factory for the purpose of resale, it is
to be treated as intermediate good.

2.2 CONCEPT AND COMPONENTS OF CONSUMPTION EXPENDITURE
2.2.1 What is Consumption Expenditure?
• In macroeconomics, consumption expenditure refers to aggregate consumption expenditure in
the economy.
2.2.2 Components of Consumption Expenditure
• The consumers of an economy are broadly classified as:
(i) Households: Households buy consumer goods for the satisfaction of their wants.
(i) The Government: The government buys consumer goods for distribution among defence
forces, for mid-day meals in the government schools, and such other purposes.
(iii) Non-profit Private Institutions (like NGOs, temples, mosques, gurudwaras, and others):
Non-profit private institutions buy consumer goods for charity.
• If we add up expenditure on the purchase of consumer goods by the households, government
and non-profit private institutions, we get an estimate of total consumption expenditure in the
Aggregate Consumption Expenditure = Consumption expenditure by the households
+ Consumption expenditure by the government
+ Consumption expenditure by the non-profit
private institutions (NGO, temples, mosques,
gurudwaras and others)

2.3.1 What is Investment?
• Investment refers to increase in the stock of capital. Thus:

• There are two components of investment:
(a) Fixed investment, and
(b) Inventory investment.
2.3.2 Components of Investment
2.3.2 (a) Fixed Investment
• Fixed investment refers to increase in the stock of fixed assets (like plant and machinery) of the
producers during an accounting year.
Example:
If at the beginning of the year 2025, a producer has a stock of 8 machines and at the end
of 2025, he has a stock of 10 machines, then the stock of his fixed assets increases by
2 machines during the year 2025.
• Therefore, fixed investment of the producer during the year 2025 = 2 machines.
• Fixed investment is also called fixed capital formation. This implies increase in the stock of capital
in terms of fixed assets (or capital goods) which are repeatedly used in the process of production
for several years.
Fixed Investment = Stock of fixed assets with the producers at the end of the accounting year

Significance of Fixed Investment
Fixed investment raises production capacity of the producers. By raising production capacity o
the producers, fixed investment leads to higher level of output in the economy.
• Higher level of output (because of fixed investment) leads to higher rate of economic growth,
popularly known as GDP growth.

2.3.2 (b) Inventory Investment
• At a point of time, producers hold the stock of
• finished goods (unsold goods),
• semi-finished goods (goods which are in the process of production), and
• raw material.
• This is called "inventory stock'. Change in inventory stock during the year is called inventory
investment of the producers.
Inventory Investment = Inventory stock at the end of the accounting year
- Inventory stock at the beginning of the accounting year
= Change in inventory stock during an accounting year
Significance of Inventory Investment
• Inventory investment primarily consists of investment in terms of the stock of (i) raw material, and
(ii) finished goods.
• The stock of raw material is significant because:
(i) It ensures uninterrupted supply of inputs to the producers.
(ii) With enough stock of raw material, the producers can avoid day-to-day purchases from the
market. Accordingly, uncertainties of the market (relating to price and availability of the raw
material) are avoided.
• The stock of finished goods is significant because it enables the producers to meet the potential
(future) demand for their product. Further, actual inventory stock at a time may not be the desired
inventory stock.
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
• Desired inventory stock refers to planned inventory stock. This is maintained by the producers to meet
the future demand.
• Undesired inventory stock, on the other hand, refers to unplanned inventory stock. It arises because
demand for the product turns out to be lower than expected. Unplanned inventory stock leads to losses.

Concept of Depreciation
• While fixed assets (like plant & machinery) are in use, they go down in value owing to
(i) normal wear and tear,
(ii) accidental damages (beyond their routine repairs and maintenance).
(i) expected obsolescence: when fixed assets become obsolete (or outdated) due to change in
technology or change in demand (which the producers normally expect to happen).
• Depreciation is the loss of value of fixed assets in use on account of: (i) normal wear and teaf,
(il) accidental damages, (ili) expected obsolescence.
• Depreciation is also called consumption of fixed capital. Because of depreciation, fixed assets
need to be replaced from time to time. Replacement of fixed assets requires funds.
34
Some Basic Concepts of Macroeconomics
• Provision for the funds is made on annual basis.
Example:
If a machine is purchased for & 10,00,000 and its expected lifetime of use is 10 years.
Then the annual provision for funds (to replace the machine after 10 years - 3 10,00,000
= 1,00,000.
This is called Depreciation Reserve Fund.
• Depreciation reserve fund is a fund to replace the worn-out fixed assets. Depreciation reserve
fund fulfills the need for replacement investment.
• Lack of depreciation reserve fund implies the lack of replacement investment. Accordingly,
overall investment (gross investment) in the economy tends to fall. This leads to a fall in the level
of output. The level of income and employment will also fall. The economy will slip into a state of
'economic slowdown'. Finally, due to the lack of depreciation reserve fund, the economy might be
caught into a low level equilibrium trap.
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
A low level equilibrium trap is a situation when:
• low income causes low demand,
• low demand, in turn, causes low output;
• low output, once again causes low income.

Expected and Unexpected Obsolescence
• Expected obsolescence has two components:
(i) Loss of value of fixed assets when these become obsolete/outdated owing to change in
technology.
A plant producing black and white TVs becomes obsolete when technology is
discovered to produce colour TVs.
(ii) Loss of value of fixed assets when these become obsolete/outdated owing to change in demand.
A plant producing rubber shoes becomes obsolete when demand shifts from rubber
shoes to leather shoes.
• Expected obsolescence is estimated by the producers on the basis of their knowledge and
experience of the market conditions.
• Unexpected obsolescence occurs owing to
(i) natural calamities (like earthquake, floods or fire), and
(ii) fall in market value of the assets when there is economic recession.
• Loss of value of fixed assets owing to unexpected obsolescence is called 'capital loss'. These
losses are not a part of depreciation or depreciation reserve fund.

2.4.2 Meaning of Flow
• A flow is a quantity measured over a specified period of time.

a day, a month, an year, etc.).

• Three phases of circular flow are as follows:

(i) Phase of Disposition/Expenditure

Phase of Production
• Production refers to 'value addition. When wood worth 75,000 is converted into chairs worth
· 10,000, there is value addition worth 7 5,000 (F 10,000 - 75,000). This is what production
means.
• Phase of production in the circular flow means the process of value addition by the producing
sector.
• The producer adds value by hiring or purchasing factors of production from the households who
are the owners of these factors (land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship).
• The factor inputs are used along with the non-factor inputs (raw material, etc.) for the production
of goods and services. Goods and services are produced for the satisfaction of human wants.
There is no end to human wants. Accordingly, there is no end to the process of production.
Phase of Income Generation (also called the Phase of Distribution)
• For rendering their factor services to the producers, the households get factor payments.
The payments can be in the following forms:
• rent for land,
• interest for capital,
• wages/salaries for labour, and
• profit for entrepreneurship.
• From the viewpoint of the households, these are factor incomes. Thus, in phase-2 of circular flow,
there is generation of income (or distribution of income) as a consequence of the production of
goods and services in phase-1. Now value addition is converted into factor income.
Phase of Disposition/Expenditure
• Purchase of final goods by the households leads to consumption expenditure. Purchase of final
goods by the producers leads to investment expenditure. Thus, in phase-3, there is disposition
(or expenditure) of income as a consequence of the generation of income in phase-2.

• Production or goods and services leads to income generation; income generation leads

once again leads to the production of goods and services.
• Thus, there is a non-stop flow of production of goods and services, generation of income a
disposition of income. Each flow keeps chasing the other flow, which is why it is called crue
flow.

2.7.4 Significance of Circular Flow Model
• Study of the circular flow of income is important due to the following reasons:
(1) Estimation of National Income: Circular flow model facilitates the estimation of national
income. National income is the sum total of factor incomes (rent + profit + wages + interest)
flowing from producers to households of a country.
It may also be defined as the market value of the goods and services flowing from producers
to other sectors of the economy. Further, it may be defined as the sum total of expenditure
on the goods and services produced by the producer sector.
(2) Knowledge of Intersectoral Interdependence: A circular flow model helps understand
interdependence among different sectors of the economy. We learn how consumers are
dependent on producers and vice versa.

Significance of the Distinction between Intermediate Goods and Final Goods
• From the viewpoint of national income estimation, the difference between intermediate goods and final
goods is very significant.
• We know, intermediate goods are those goods which are purchased by one firm from the other either
for resale or for use as raw material in the production of other goods and services. When these goods
are used as raw material in the production of final goods, the value of intermediate goods is reflected
in the value of final goods.
• To illustrate, firm A bought cloth for * 5,000 to be used as raw material in the production of shirts.
• The shirts were sold for ‹ 7,000. This value of? 7,000 includes the value of cloth, viz., 7 5,000.
Therefore, in the calculation of national income, the value of only final goods, that is, shirts of
* 7,000 would be included.
• The value of cloth (<5,000) is the value of intermediate goods (= intermediate cost or intermediate
consumption) and hence, will not be included in national product/national income. If we include
the value of intermediate goods also, the value of national product would add up to * 12,000
(* 7,000 + F 5,000). It causes double counting. Because, the value of cloth * 5,000) is already
included in the value of shirts (<7,000).
Thus, in the calculation of national product/national income, the value of only final goods is taken into
account.

Injections
These are those macro variables, a rise in the level of which leads to a rise in the level of outin,
economy. These include:
) government consumption expenditure,
(ii) government investment expenditure, and
(il) exports (expenditure on domestic product by the foreigners).
• A rise in the level of any of these variables implies a rise in the level of demand for the goods produce,
in the domestic economy. This is expected to cause a rise in the level of output in the economy. This
called expansion of circular flow.
Leakages/Withdrawals
These are those macro variables, a rise in the level of which leads to a fall in the level of output in the
economy. These include:
) saving (opposite of consumption),
(il) government taxes (opposite of government investment), and
(il) imports (opposite of exports).
• A rise in the level of any of these variables implies a fall in the level of demand for the domestically produced
goods. This leads to a fall in the level of output in the economy. This is called contraction of circulario.
The circular flow of income remains stable if 'leakages' are exactly equal to 'injections.
Why does the Circular Flow of Money never Stop?
This may be explained in terms of the twin demand-supply relationship' between producers and the
households. Households will always demand goods and services from the producers, and will avays
supply them their factor services.
• It is by selling their factor services that the households earn money to buy goods and services.
• On the other hand, producers will always demand factor services from the households, and will alvays
supply them the goods and services.
• it is only by selling the goods and services to the households that the producers earn money to
buy factor services.
human beings. Accordingly, the circular flow of money never stops.
Power Points [Summary of the Chapter]
• Classification of Goods
• Final Goods are those goods which have crost ed the boundary line of production, and are read
Tor use by their final users. For example shoes used by the households, or tractor used by th
Tarmers, Final goods must lead to either final consumption expenditure or investment expenditure
in the economy. Final goods are of two types:
() Consumption Goods: Consumption goods are those goods which are directly used for the
satisfaction of human wants. Example: Milk and ice cream used by the households.
Some Basic Concepts of Macroeconomics
(ii) Capital Goods: Capital goods are fixed assets of the producers and are repeatedly used in
the process of production. These are durable-use producer goods and are of high value.
Example: Plant and machinery.
• Intermediate Goods are those goods which are purchased by one firm from the other for resale or
for use as raw material in the production of other goods. Example: Wood used in the production
of chairs.
• Consumption Expenditure is the aggregate consumption expenditure in the economy. It has three
components: (i) Consumption expenditure by the households, (ii) Consumption expenditure by the
government, (iii) Consumption expenditure by the non-profit private institutions.
• Investment is a process of adding to the stock of capital. It has two components:
(i) Fixed Investment: Fixed Investment is addition to the stock of fixed assets of the producers
during an accounting year.
(i) Inventory Investment: Inventory Investment is addition to the stock of inventory with the
producers during an accounting year.
• Gross Investment is the expenditure on the purchase of fixed assets and expenditure on the inventory
stock of the producers during the accounting year.
• Net Investment refers to increase in the stock of capital during an accounting year.
Net Investment = Gross investment - Depreciation
Depreciation (also called consumption of fixed capital) refers to loss of value of fixed assets in use,
on account of: (i) normal wear and tear, (ii) accidental damages, and (il) expected (or foreseen)
obsolescence.
• Depreciation Reserve Fund refers to that fund which the producers keep to cope with depreciation
losses in the process of production.
• Stocks are the quantities which are measured at a point of time. Example: Your balance in the bank
account as on January 1, 2026.
Flows are the quantities which are measured over a specified period of time. Example: Your income
per month.
L Four Sectors of the Economy
• Household Sector refers to consumers engaged in the consumption of goods and services.
• Producing Sector refers to all producing units (or firms) in the economy.
• Government Sector refers to government as a welfare agency (engaged in maintaining law and
order, defence, and other services of public welfare), It also refers to government as a producer.
• The External Sector also called 'Rest of the World Sector', is engaged in the export and import of
goods and the flow of capital between the domestic economy and rest of the world.
• Circular Flow of Income refers to the circularity of the flows of production, income and expenditure
across different sectors of the economy.
• Real Flows refer to the flow of goods and services across different sectors of the economy.
• Money Flows refer to the flow of money (in terms of receipts and payments) across different
sectors of the economy.
• Significance: Circular flow models are significant as they; (i) facilitate estimation of national
income, and (i) show interdependence among different sectors highlighting circularity of
intersectoral flows.

End-use Classification of Goods
• End-use classification of goods is that classification which classifies goods on the basis of their
end-use and end-users, rather than their physical characteristics.
- Goods are classified as 'Final Goods' when goods have crossed the boundary line of production, and
are ready for use by their final users.
- Goods are classified as 'Intermediate Goods' when goods are within the boundary line of production
and are not ready for use by their final users.
- Good are classified as 'Consumer Goods' when goods are used for the direct satisfaction of households.
- Goods are classified as 'Capital Goods' when goods are used as fixed assets by the producers.

of goods produced in this sector.
• It is used to distinguish final goods from intermediate goods.

What do we mean when we say that final goods have crossed the boundary line of production?
• We mean that these goods are out of the process of production or the process of value addition,
and have reached their final users.
A shirt in a retail showroom is all set for sale to its final user. No value is to be added to the
shirt by way of stitching, ironing, packaging, etc.
Is it to be treated as a final good?
"No' should be the answer. Because:
The final stage of value addition occurs only when the shirt is finally sold to the consumer
(the final user), If the retailer buys the shirt for & 800 and sells to the consumer for 7 1,000,
there is value addition of & 200.
To repeat, the value addition process is completed only when the product reaches its final
user: it may be a shirt purchased by the consumer, or a tractor purchased by a farmer (Both,
the consumer and the farmer are the final users).
• You may note that only final goods are included in the estimation of national product or
national income.
2.1.1 (a) Consumption Goods or Consumer Goods
• Consumption goods (or consumer goods) are those goods which are directly used for the
satisfaction of human wants.
Example:
Ice cream and milk as used by the households. These goods are consumed by the households
when purchased.

2.1.1 (b) Capital Goods
• Capital goods are fixed assets of the producers. Plant and machinery is an example of capital
goods. As fixed assets, capital goods are repeatedly used in the process of production for several
years and are of high value. Even nuts and bolts are used for several years, but these are not
capital goods as these are of low value. Only those fixed assets of the producers are taken as
capital goods which are used in the process of production for several years and which are of
high value.
• Also, capital goods involve depreciation. Depreciation refers to loss of value of fixed assets (in
use) owing to their wear and tear.
• These goods are used by the producers either for:
(i) the replacement of the existing capital stock, or for
(ii) addition to the capital stock.
DID YOU KNOW
All Machines are not Capital Goods, for example:
• A sewing machine in a tailoring shop is a fixed asset of the tailor; it is a capital good.
• But the same machine with a consumer household is not a capital good. It is simply a durable-use
consumer good.
• Likewise, a car with a tourist company is a capital good. But the same car with a household is a
durable-use consumer good.
• Thus, while identifying goods as capital goods, we must make sure about their end-user.
- If the end-user of a durable good is a household consumer, it is durable-use consumer good.
- On the other hand, if the end-user of a durable good is a producer, it is a capital good.
Finally, capital goods are only those durable goods which are used as producer goods, not as
consumer goods.

boxes.title: CRITICAL QUESTIONS
boxes.text:
Q. 1. All producer goods are not capital goods. Why?
Ans. Producer goods include:
(i) goods used as fixed assets, like plant and machinery, and
(ii) goods used as raw material, like wood used to make furniture.
Capital goods include only fixed assets of the producers. These are durable-use producer goods.
On the other hand, goods used as raw material are single-use producer goods. These are not
repeatedly used in the process of product
dingly, all producer goods are not capital goods.
28
Some Basic Concepts of Macroeconomics
Q. 2. Classify the following as capital good or consumer good:
(i) Car purchased by a driver to be used as a taxi
(i) Cloth lying unsold with a trader at the end of an year
(ili) Sugar used by households
(iv) Services of a doctor or a lawyer used by a household
(v) Laptop purchased by a household
(vi) Machine purchased by a sugar mill
Ans. Capital Good: (i), (ii) [as a part of capital stock], (vi)
Consumer Good: (iii), (iv), (v)
2.1.2 Intermediate Goods
• Intermediate goods are those goods
(i) which have yet not crossed the boundary line of production,
(ii) value is still to be added to these goods, and
(iii) which are yet not ready for use by their final users.
• In other words, intermediate goods are those goods which are purchased by one firm from the
other firm: (i) as raw material, or (ii) as goods for resale.
Example:
(i) Wood purchased by a carpenter (from a timber merchant) for making chairs is an
intermediate good. Because, wood is used as a raw material for making chairs. Value is
to be added to wood by converting it into chairs.
(ii) Shirts purchased by firm X from firm Y for resale are intermediate goods. Because, value
is to be added to the shirts through resale.
• Non-inclusion in National Income: Value of intermediate goods ultimately becomes a part of the
value of final goods.
• Accordingly, intermediate goods are not included in the
estimation of national product or
national income.
• Otherwise, there would be duplication in the estimation of national product, called 'Double
Counting' (counting the value of a good more than once).
Example:
When a carpenter buys wood worth 10,000 and converts it into chairs worth & 20,000,
then the value of chairs (final goods) includes the value of wood (intermediate good). If we
add R 10,000 (wood) + R 20,000 (chairs), the total becomes & 30,000. Thus, leading to double
counting ofF 10,000.
• Expenditure on Intermediate Goods: Expenditure on intermediate goods by the producers
during an accounting year is called intermediate consumption or intermediate cost.
Same Good May be Final or Intermediate
• It is not possible to name one set of goods as final goods and another set as intermediate goods.
The same good may be final or intermediate good. The distinction depends on the end-use of the
goods.
29

Q. 3. How would you find out whether a particular expenditure is an expenditure on intermediate
goods or on final goods?
Ans. Expenditure on final goods must lead to:
(i) final consumption expenditure (C), or
(il) investment expenditure (I).
The expenditure which does not lead to C and I (like the expenditure on raw material) is to be
treated as an expenditure on intermediate goods. Expenditure on intermediate goods leads to
intermediate consumption or intermediate cost.
30
Some Basic Concepts of Macroeconomics
Q. 4. Purchase of a car always means the purchase of a final good. Do you agree?
Ans. No. It depends on the end-use of the car. If it is purchased by a household, it is a final good. It is
like a consumer durable.
If it is purchased by taxi-operators, then again it is a final good, as it is to be finally used by the
producer as a fixed asset.
However, if the car is purchased by a retail dealer from the factory for the purpose of resale, it is
to be treated as intermediate good.

A low level equilibrium trap is a situation when:
• low income causes low demand,
• low demand, in turn, causes low output;
• low output, once again causes low income.
irap
Expected and Unexpected Obsolescence
• Expected obsolescence has two components:
(i) Loss of value of fixed assets when these become obsolete/outdated owing to change in
technology.
A plant producing black and white TVs becomes obsolete when technology is
discovered to produce colour TVs.
(ii) Loss of value of fixed assets when these become obsolete/outdated owing to change in demand.
A plant producing rubber shoes becomes obsolete when demand shifts from rubber
shoes to leather shoes.
• Expected obsolescence is estimated by the producers on the basis of their knowledge and
experience of the market conditions.
• Unexpected obsolescence occurs owing to
(i) natural calamities (like earthquake, floods or fire), and
(ii) fall in market value of the assets when there is economic recession.
• Loss of value of fixed assets owing to unexpected obsolescence is called 'capital loss'. These
losses are not a part of depreciation or depreciation reserve fund.
[Note: Only expected obsolescence is considered for the estimation of depreciation, not the unexpected

boxes.title: CRITICAL QUESTIONS
boxes.text:
Q. 6. How does higher rate of net capital formation lead to higher level of productivity/efficiency of
Ans. Higher rate of net capital formation implies greater availability of capital (in terms of machines)
per unit of labour. Aided by machines, efficiency of labour definitely increases. This precisely is
the reason why labour in developed countries (like USA) is more efficient than in less developed
countries like India.
Q. 7. Distinguish between depreciation and depreciation reserve fund.
Ans. Depreciation is the loss of fixed assets in use on account of: (i) normal wear and tear,
(ii) accidental damages, and (iii) expecte
seen obsolescence.
36
Some Basic Concepts of Macroeconomics
On the other hand, depreciation reserve fund is a provision of funds to cope with depreciation
losses. These funds are used for the replacement of fixed assets when these are worn-out or
when these become obsolete/outdated.
Q. 8. What is current replacement cost?
Ans. It refers to the estimated value of depreciation for all the producing units in the economy, during
the period of an accounting year.

Q. 10. Are the following Stocks or Flows? Explain with a reason.

Consumption of Sugar, (v) Services of a Tutor, (vi) Production of Cement, (vii) Machinery of a
(i) Investment: It is a flow concept because it is related to a period of time.
(ii) Monetary Expenditure: It is a flow concept because it is related to a period of time.
(ii) A Hundred Rupee Note: It is a stock concept because it is a component of supply of money.

Q. 11. Based on the following headlines, identify whether each item is a stock or flow variable:
(a) "Gross GST revenue collections reached & 2.1 lakh crore in April 2025, reflecting strong
economic activity and better compliance under GST 2.0."
(b) "The GST Council has approved a rationalised two-rate structure under GST 2.0-5% and
18%—to simplify taxation and reduce the burden on consumers."
AnS.
(a) Flow variable-Because GST revenue is collected over a period of time (one month, April
2025).
(b) Stock variable-Because the GST rate structure exists at a specific point in time and does
not depend on a time period.
Q. 12. Are exports and imports stock variables or flow variables?
Ans. Certain concepts in economics are studied only as flow variables, not as stock variables. Exports
and imports are always flow variables.

boxes.title: ABILITY ZONE
boxes.text:
Significance of the Distinction between Intermediate Goods and Final Goods
• From the viewpoint of national income estimation, the difference between intermediate goods and final
goods is very significant.
• We know, intermediate goods are those goods which are purchased by one firm from the other either
for resale or for use as raw material in the production of other goods and services. When these goods
are used as raw material in the production of final goods, the value of intermediate goods is reflected
in the value of final goods.
• To illustrate, firm A bought cloth for * 5,000 to be used as raw material in the production of shirts.
• The shirts were sold for ‹ 7,000. This value of? 7,000 includes the value of cloth, viz., 7 5,000.
Therefore, in the calculation of national income, the value of only final goods, that is, shirts of
* 7,000 would be included.
• The value of cloth (<5,000) is the value of intermediate goods (= intermediate cost or intermediate
consumption) and hence, will not be included in national product/national income. If we include
the value of intermediate goods also, the value of national product would add up to * 12,000
(* 7,000 + F 5,000). It causes double counting. Because, the value of cloth * 5,000) is already
included in the value of shirts (<7,000).
Thus, in the calculation of national product/national income, the value of only final goods is taken into
account.

boxes.title: Power Points [Summary of the Chapter]
boxes.text:
• Classification of Goods
• Final Goods are those goods which have crost ed the boundary line of production, and are read
Tor use by their final users. For example shoes used by the households, or tractor used by th
Tarmers, Final goods must lead to either final consumption expenditure or investment expenditure
in the economy. Final goods are of two types:
() Consumption Goods: Consumption goods are those goods which are directly used for the
satisfaction of human wants. Example: Milk and ice cream used by the households.
Some Basic Concepts of Macroeconomics
(ii) Capital Goods: Capital goods are fixed assets of the producers and are repeatedly used in
the process of production. These are durable-use producer goods and are of high value.
Example: Plant and machinery.
• Intermediate Goods are those goods which are purchased by one firm from the other for resale or
for use as raw material in the production of other goods. Example: Wood used in the production
of chairs.
• Consumption Expenditure is the aggregate consumption expenditure in the economy. It has three
components: (i) Consumption expenditure by the households, (ii) Consumption expenditure by the
government, (iii) Consumption expenditure by the non-profit private institutions.
• Investment is a process of adding to the stock of capital. It has two components:
(i) Fixed Investment: Fixed Investment is addition to the stock of fixed assets of the producers
during an accounting year.
(i) Inventory Investment: Inventory Investment is addition to the stock of inventory with the
producers during an accounting year.
• Gross Investment is the expenditure on the purchase of fixed assets and expenditure on the inventory
stock of the producers during the accounting year.
• Net Investment refers to increase in the stock of capital during an accounting year.
Net Investment = Gross investment - Depreciation
Depreciation (also called consumption of fixed capital) refers to loss of value of fixed assets in use,
on account of: (i) normal wear and tear, (ii) accidental damages, and (il) expected (or foreseen)
obsolescence.
• Depreciation Reserve Fund refers to that fund which the producers keep to cope with depreciation
losses in the process of production.
• Stocks are the quantities which are measured at a point of time. Example: Your balance in the bank
account as on January 1, 2026.
Flows are the quantities which are measured over a specified period of time. Example: Your income
per month.
L Four Sectors of the Economy
• Household Sector refers to consumers engaged in the consumption of goods and services.
• Producing Sector refers to all producing units (or firms) in the economy.
• Government Sector refers to government as a welfare agency (engaged in maintaining law and
order, defence, and other services of public welfare), It also refers to government as a producer.
• The External Sector also called 'Rest of the World Sector', is engaged in the export and import of
goods and the flow of capital between the domestic economy and rest of the world.
• Circular Flow of Income refers to the circularity of the flows of production, income and expenditure
across different sectors of the economy.
• Real Flows refer to the flow of goods and services across different sectors of the economy.
• Money Flows refer to the flow of money (in terms of receipts and payments) across different
sectors of the economy.
• Significance: Circular flow models are significant as they; (i) facilitate estimation of national
income, and (i) show interdependence among different sectors highlighting circularity of
intersectoral flows.

title: National Income and Related Aggregates
intro: National income is the sum total of factor incomes earned by normal residents of a country during the period of an accounting year.

lessons.title: National income, factor incomes and transfer incomes
lessons.body: National income is the sum total of factor incomes earned by normal residents of a country during the period of an accounting year. Factor incomes are rewards for factor services: compensation of employees, rent, interest and profit. Transfer incomes such as gifts, charity and old-age pensions are unilateral receipts without a current productive service in return; they are excluded. An employer’s retirement pension earned through service differs from an old-age welfare pension.

lessons.title: Normal residents and domestic territory
lessons.body: A normal resident ordinarily resides in a country and has a centre of economic interest there. Citizenship alone does not determine residence. Tourists and visitors for medical treatment do not become residents merely through travel. Diplomats remain residents of their home countries; border workers are residents where they live. Domestic territory is economic territory: Indian embassies abroad belong to India’s domestic territory; foreign embassies in India do not. Check the Ability Zone for ships, aircraft, fishing vessels and other special cases.

lessons.title: Domestic income versus national income
lessons.body: Domestic income is the sum total of factor incomes generated within the domestic territory, whether earned by residents or non-residents. National income belongs to normal residents, wherever earned. Net factor income from abroad is factor income received from the rest of the world minus factor income paid to the rest of the world. Remittances that are gifts are transfers, not NFIA.
lessons.formula:
NNP at FC = NDP at FC + NFIA
NFIA = Factor income from abroad − Factor income to abroad
lessons.textbookHeading: 3.2 DOMESTIC AND NATIONAL CONCEPTS OF INCOME

lessons.title: The three conversion bridges
lessons.body: Use three independent adjustments. Gross to net: subtract depreciation. Domestic to national: add NFIA. Market price to factor cost: subtract net indirect taxes, which equal indirect taxes minus subsidies. Reverse the sign when travelling backwards. A negative NFIA reduces national income; negative NIT means subsidies exceed indirect taxes. Do not deduct indirect taxes again if NIT is already supplied.
lessons.formula:
NNPFC = GDPMP − Depreciation − NIT + NFIA
GDPMP = NNPFC + Depreciation + NIT − NFIA
lessons.textbookHeading: 3.3 GROSS AND NET · 3.4 MARKET PRICE AND FACTOR COST

lessons.title: Eight related aggregates
lessons.body: GDPMP, GDPFC, NDPMP and NDPFC are domestic measures; GNPMP, GNPFC, NNPMP and NNPFC are national measures. Gross measures include consumption of fixed capital; net measures exclude it. Market-price measures include net indirect taxes; factor-cost measures exclude them. National income means NNPFC; domestic income means NDPFC. Identify all three labels before substituting a number.

lessons.title: Nominal GDP, real GDP and GDP deflator
lessons.body: Nominal GDP is valued at current-year prices; real GDP is valued at base-year prices. Real GDP helps isolate changes in physical production from changes in prices. Nominal GDP may rise with unchanged output simply because prices rise. The GDP deflator is the ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP multiplied by 100. Use the price index as a percentage index, not as a decimal, in the formula below.
lessons.formula:
Nominal GDP = Σ(Current price × Current quantity)
Real GDP = Σ(Base-year price × Current quantity)
GDP deflator = Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP × 100
Real GDP = Nominal GDP ÷ GDP deflator × 100

lessons.title: GDP and welfare: why output is an incomplete measure
lessons.body: A rise in real GDP can expand available goods and services, but it does not ensure an equal rise in welfare. The textbook highlights distribution of income, composition of GDP, non-monetary transactions and externalities. Unequal distribution can leave most people without gains; more military goods may not improve consumption; unpaid household work is omitted; pollution imposes an unpriced cost. Positive externalities are benefits not paid for; negative externalities are costs not compensated.

lessons.title: Special cases of residents and territory
lessons.textbookHeading: ABILITY ZONE · Normal Residents of a Country · Components of Domestic Territory
lessons.body: Normal Residents: citizens of another country can be residents here when their centre of economic interest is here; officials and diplomats serving abroad remain residents of their home country; border workers are residents where they live. Domestic Territory: include a country’s embassies, consulates and military establishments abroad, ships and aircraft operated by its residents between countries, and fishing vessels and floating platforms operated by residents in international waters under the accounting conventions. Exclude foreign embassies and international organisations located inside its political borders. Residence and territory are separate tests.

Introductory Macroeconomics
3.1 CONCEPT OF NATIONAL INCOME
3.1.1 Meaning of National Income
• National income is the sum total of factor incomes earned by normal residents of a country
during the period of an accounting year. This dehniton of national income conveys two
important points:
(i) national income includes factor incomes only, and
i) national income includes income of only the normal residents of a country.
Let us go deeper into the concepts of (i) factor incomes, and (i) normal residents.
3.1.2 Concept of Factor Incomes
• Factor incomes are the payments made by the producing units (firms) to the households (owners
of the factors of production) for the use of their factor services.
• Factor incomes (or factor payments) are broadly classified as under:
(i) Compensation of employees (received by the households for rendering their services as
employees of the producing units).
(i) Rent (received by the households for the use of their land by the producing units).
(i) Interest (received by the households for the use of their capital by the producing units).
(iv) Profit (received by the households for the use of their entrepreneurial skills by the producing
• In the estimation of national income, we include only these factor incomes or factor
payments).
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Factor Payment = Factor Income
• Factor payments and factor incomes are two ways of looking at the same concept. Hence, these are
used interchangeably.
• Factor payments refer to payments made by the producers to the households for the use of their factor
• Factor incomes on the other hand refer to the income (payment) received by the households for
rendering their factor services to the producers.
Factor Incomes are Different from Transfer Incomes
• Transfer incomes are those incomes which are received by a person as help, donation, charity
* As transter incomes are unearne a countrye, i.e., not earned as rewards for rendering facto
services, these are not included in the estimation of national income.

3.1.3 Concept of Normal Residents
Who are normal residents of a country?
A normal resident is said to be one:
• who ordinarily resides in the country concerned (for one year or more), and
• whose centre of economic interest lies in that country.
Here, note these observations carefully:
(i) A person residing in a country for a period of one year (or more) is taken as 'ordinarily
residing' in that country. This person may or may not be the citizen of that country.
(ii) A person is said to have his economic interest in a country when he considers that country
as a central place of all his economic activities (production, consumption and investment).
Examples:
Indians working in foreign embassies in India.
Indians employed in World Health Organisation located in India.

3.2.2 Concept of Domestic Territory of a Country
• In common language, the domestic territory of a country is understood to mean political territory
of a nation. But, in economics, it refers to 'economic territory' which is a much wider concept than
political territory.
• According to United Nations, "Economic territory is the geographical territory administered by a
government within which persons, goods and capital circulate freely!"
• The above definition raises two critical questions:
Do we have this freedom of circulation (of persons, goods and capital) in the embassies of foreign
countries located in India?
The answer is 'No'.
Do we have this freedom of circulation (of persons, goods and capital) in Indian embassies located
abroad?
The answer is "Yes'.
Accordingly, we conclude that foreign embassies located in India are not a part of domestic/
economic territory of India. On the other hand, Indian embassies located abroad are a part of
domestic/economic territory of India.
Thus, while defining the term domestic territory, the focus is NOT to be on political boundaries of a
nation but on the geographical area where our persons, our goods and our capital enjoy the freedom
of circulation.

3.2.3 Conversion of Domestic Income into National Income
Before we understand how to convert domestic income into national income and vice versa, it is
important to note that:
• our domestic income includes factor income earned by non-residents within the domestic
territory of our country,
• our domestic income does not include factor income earned by our residents from the domestic
territories of other countries.
Accordingly, domestic income becomes national income provided:
• We exclude from domestic income that part of factor income which belongs to non-residents within
our domestic territory, and
• We add to domestic income that part of factor income which our residents earn from rest of the
world (or from the domestic territories of other countries).

where goods, services or resources are exchanged without the use of money as a media.
of exchange. In rural economies, barter system of exchange still prevails to some exten
Payments for farm labour are often made in kind rather than in cash.

Q. 10. What lowers the significance of GDP as an index of welfare?
Ans. The following observations explain how the significance of GDP as an index of welfare is lowered:
(i) Distribution of Income: GDP as an index of welfare loses significance if the distribution of
income turns unequal.
(ii) Composition of GDP: If luxuries are produced for richer sections of the society and the poor
suffer deprivation, GDP growth becomes meaningless.
(ili) Non-monetary Exchanges/Transactions: Larger the non-monetary transactions, greater the
underestimation of GDP as an index of welfare.
(iv) Externalities: GDP index does not account for externalities: the good and bad impact
of economic activities without the price or penalty. Environmental pollution related to
production activity is an important example. This also lowers the significance of GDP as an
index of welfare.
Q. 11. "GDP growth as an index of welfare loses its significance if there is a deep economic divide in
the economy." State whether true or false and provide a reason for the same.
Ans. True. Economic divide indicates the gulf between the rich and the poor. If the gulf increases, GDP
growth loses its significance.

• It is not necessary that normal resident of a country is also a citizen of that country. A person may be a
normal resident of one country even when he is a citizen of other country.
• Normal Residents of a country include:
• Citizens (and institutions) of the country who normally reside in the country and whose centre
of economic interest lies in the country.
• Citizens of other nations who continue to live in the country beyond a period of one year and
whose centre of economic interest lies in the country.
• For example, if an Indian is living in USA for more than one year and his centre of economic
interest lies in that country, he would be deemed as a normal resident of USA even when he
continues to be a citizen of India.
• Citizens of a country working in international organisations (like World Bank and IMF) or foreign
embassies located in that country.
• For example, an Indian working in the World Bank office located in New Delhi would be
considered as a normal resident of India.
• Citizens of a country who are living abroad, but not for a period exceeding one year and whose
centre of economic interest lies in their home country.
• Border workers or persons who cross the border between two countries daily or regularly in
order to work in one country are the residents of the country in which they live, not of the country
in which they are working.
• Officials, diplomats, and members of the armed forces of a foreign country are treated as the
normal residents of the country to which they belong, and not of the country in which they are
employed.

Concept of Green GNP
• GNP (at current or constant prices) is estimated with no regard to (i) environmental pollution, and
(ii) exploitation of natural resources.
• If GNP increases along with increase in environmental pollution, the quality of life would be far less
than indicated by the index of GNP. Likewise, if GNP increases along with excessive exploitation of the
natural resources (so excessive that it reduces availability of resources for the future generations), the
increase in GNP would only be misleading as it cannot be sustained in the years to come.
• Accordingly, it is suggested that GNP index should account for (i) cost in terms of environmental
pollution, and (i) cost in terms of excessive exploitation of natural resources. Estimation of GNP that
accounts for these parameters (environmental pollution and excessive exploitation of natural resources)
is called Green GNP.
New Concepts Introduced by CSO (Central Statistics Office)
• In India, national income and related aggregates are defined and estimated by CSO. Since 2015,
CSO has introduced some new concepts as under:
• Net Production Taxes:
Net Production Taxes = Production taxes - Production subsidies

registration fee may be cited as examples.
• Net Product Taxes:
Net Product Taxes = Product taxes - Product subsidies
> To be noted, product taxes and product subsidies are paid and received per unit of product.
Excise tax, service tax may be cited as examples.
• Basic Price
> Basic price includes production taxes and production subsidies only. Categorically, basic
price does not include product taxes and product subsidies.
• GVA at Basic Price
> CSO now estimates GVA (gross value added) at basic price. To be noted, GVA at basic price
accounts only for production taxes and production subsidies. It does not account for product
taxes and product subsidies.
• Difference among GVA at Factor Cost, GVA at Basic Price and GVA at Market Price
GVA at factor cost + Net production taxes = GVA at Basic Price
GVA at basic price + Net product taxes = GVA at Market Price

3.1.3 Concept of Normal Residents
Who are normal residents of a country?
A normal resident is said to be one:
• who ordinarily resides in the country concerned (for one year or more), and
• whose centre of economic interest lies in that country.
Here, note these observations carefully:
(i) A person residing in a country for a period of one year (or more) is taken as 'ordinarily
residing' in that country. This person may or may not be the citizen of that country.
(ii) A person is said to have his economic interest in a country when he considers that country
as a central place of all his economic activities (production, consumption and investment).
Examples:
Indians working in foreign embassies in India.
Indians employed in World Health Organisation located in India.
The foreign citizens living in India for a period of more than one year (other than
those for studies or medical treatment).
[Note: National income includes income of only the normal residents of a country. It does not include
income of the non-residents, even when they happen to be the citizens of our country.

boxes.text:
Q. 10. What lowers the significance of GDP as an index of welfare?
Ans. The following observations explain how the significance of GDP as an index of welfare is lowered:
(i) Distribution of Income: GDP as an index of welfare loses significance if the distribution of
income turns unequal.
(ii) Composition of GDP: If luxuries are produced for richer sections of the society and the poor
suffer deprivation, GDP growth becomes meaningless.
(ili) Non-monetary Exchanges/Transactions: Larger the non-monetary transactions, greater the
underestimation of GDP as an index of welfare.
(iv) Externalities: GDP index does not account for externalities: the good and bad impact
of economic activities without the price or penalty. Environmental pollution related to
production activity is an important example. This also lowers the significance of GDP as an
index of welfare.
Q. 11. "GDP growth as an index of welfare loses its significance if there is a deep economic divide in
the economy." State whether true or false and provide a reason for the same.
Ans. True. Economic divide indicates the gulf between the rich and the poor. If the gulf increases, GDP
growth loses its significance.

boxes.title: ABILITY ZONE
boxes.text:
Normal Residents of a Country
• It is not necessary that normal resident of a country is also a citizen of that country. A person may be a
normal resident of one country even when he is a citizen of other country.
• Normal Residents of a country include:
• Citizens (and institutions) of the country who normally reside in the country and whose centre
of economic interest lies in the country.
• Citizens of other nations who continue to live in the country beyond a period of one year and
whose centre of economic interest lies in the country.
• For example, if an Indian is living in USA for more than one year and his centre of economic
interest lies in that country, he would be deemed as a normal resident of USA even when he
continues to be a citizen of India.
• Citizens of a country working in international organisations (like World Bank and IMF) or foreign
embassies located in that country.
• For example, an Indian working in the World Bank office located in New Delhi would be
considered as a normal resident of India.
• Citizens of a country who are living abroad, but not for a period exceeding one year and whose
centre of economic interest lies in their home country.
• Border workers or persons who cross the border between two countries daily or regularly in
order to work in one country are the residents of the country in which they live, not of the country
in which they are working.
• Officials, diplomats, and members of the armed forces of a foreign country are treated as the
normal residents of the country to which they belong, and not of the country in which they are
employed.
