title: Measurement of National Income
intro: Value added is value of output minus intermediate consumption.

lessons.title: Value added method: measure production once
lessons.body: Value added is value of output minus intermediate consumption. Value of output equals sales plus change in stock, with own-account production added where applicable. Sum GVA at market price across producing units to obtain GDPMP. Deduct depreciation and NIT, then add NFIA for national income. Alternatively, sum sectoral NVAFC and add NFIA.
lessons.formula:
Value of output = Sales + Closing stock − Opening stock
GVA MP = Value of output − Intermediate consumption
NNPFC = ΣGVA MP − Depreciation − NIT + NFIA

lessons.title: Double counting and value-added precautions
lessons.body: Double counting means counting the value of the same output more than once. Avoid it by counting final goods only or summing value added at each stage. If wheat sells for 100, flour for 160 and bread for 250, total value added is 100 + 60 + 90 = 250, not 510. Include own-account construction and imputed rent of owner-occupied houses. Exclude resale value of second-hand goods, but include the current broker’s service. Do not count intermediate goods separately from the final product.

lessons.title: Income method: compensation, surplus and mixed income
lessons.body: Income method measures domestic income as the sum total of factor incomes generated within domestic territory. Compensation of employees includes wages and salaries in cash and kind and employers’ social-security contributions. Operating surplus comprises rent and royalty, interest and profit. Profit includes corporate tax, dividends and retained earnings; these are components, so do not add them again if total profit is given. Mixed income of the self-employed combines labour and property income that cannot be separated.
lessons.formula:
NDPFC = Compensation of employees + Operating surplus + Mixed income
Operating surplus = Rent and royalty + Interest + Profit
National income = NDPFC + NFIA

lessons.title: Income-method precautions
lessons.body: Include only incomes earned from current productive services. Exclude transfer receipts, capital gains and windfall gains. Exclude interest on consumption loans and interest on public debt when it represents a transfer rather than payment for a productive service, following the textbook treatment. Include imputed rent and production for self-consumption where measured. Do not count sale proceeds of shares or second-hand goods as factor income; the current commission or brokerage is a service income.

lessons.title: Expenditure method and its precautions
lessons.body: Expenditure method measures final expenditure on domestically produced output. Add private final consumption expenditure, government final consumption expenditure, gross domestic capital formation and net exports. Gross domestic capital formation includes fixed capital formation and change in stocks. Exclude financial-asset purchases, transfers and second-hand purchases; include current brokerage. Subtract imports because imported content may already be included in consumption or investment. Do not add change in stock twice if gross domestic capital formation already includes it.
lessons.formula:
GDPMP = PFCE + GFCE + GDCF + (X − M)
NNPFC = PFCE + GFCE + GDCF + (X − M) − Depreciation − NIT + NFIA

lessons.title: Reconciliation and treatment of tricky items
lessons.body: The three methods measure the same current production from different sides: value added creates factor income, and income finances final expenditure. In an exam, classify each item before calculating. Government services are counted even when provided free; employer provident-fund contributions belong in compensation. Scholarships and welfare pensions are transfers. Foreign factor earnings require a residence/territory check; the purchase of a newly produced house is investment. Read the supplied transaction table for item-by-item domestic and national treatment.
lessons.textbookHeading: 4.5 RECONCILIATION OF THREE METHODS · 4.6 TREATMENT OF DIFFERENT ITEMS

lessons.title: Steps under the three measurement methods
lessons.body: Value Added Method: identify and classify producing units; estimate each unit’s output and intermediate consumption; obtain sectoral value added; aggregate and make depreciation, tax and NFIA adjustments to national income. Income Method: identify producing enterprises; classify factor incomes into compensation, operating surplus and mixed income; sum them to obtain domestic income; add NFIA. Expenditure Method: identify final expenditure by sectors; classify consumption, investment and net exports; sum to GDPMP; convert to NNPFC. Keep the starting aggregate clear because the adjustments depend on whether it is gross/net and market price/factor cost.

The problem of double counting is avoided in case either of the following two methods is adopted
for the estimation of GDP:
(i) Final Output Method: According to this method, only final goods and services (in terms of
their end-use) are to be considered in the estimation of GDP. Intermediate goods are not to
be considered.

boundary line of production and which are ready for use by their final users who may be
consumers or producers. Intermediate goods are not to be considered, as these are within
the boundary line of production and are yet not ready for use by their final users.
> In the above example, the bread sold to the consumers is the final good. Only the value of
final good (bread sold to the consumers, in the present case), i.e., & 900 will be included
in the estimation of GDP.

output or sales) by all the producing units is to be considered in the estimation of GDP.

Q. 4. How do you distinguish between old-age persions and retirement pensions in the context of
estimation of national income?
Ans. Old-age pensions are unilateral payments or transfer payments. These are not included in the
estimation of national income. On the other hand, retirement pensions are like a deferred
wage. These are related to factor services rendered by the recipients prior to their retirement.
Accordingly, these are included in the estimation of national income,
Methods of Calculating National Income
Q. 5. Operating surplus does not arise in (i) subsistence sector, and (i) general government sector of
the economy. Why?
Ans. Operating surplus does not arise in the subsistence sector and in the general government sector
because of the following reasons:
(i) In the subsistence sector, production is meant only for subsistence of the producing families.
Production is not meant for sale in the market. There is no marketable surplus. Accordingly,
there is no operating surplus.
(ii) In the general government sector, production is meant only for collective consumption (or
consumption by the general public). Goods and services are produced not for sale in the
market, but for general welfare of the people.
Example: Services of law & order and defence are available to the people free of charge.
Accordingly, there is no operating surplus in the 'general government" sector.
Q. 6. How are dividends, corporate taxes and undistributed profits treated in national income?
Ans. (i) Dividends: These are included in the estimation of national income as these are a part of
factor payments.
(ii) Corporate Taxes: These are not included, as all taxes are transfer payments.
(iii) Undistributed Profits: These are retained earnings of the firms and are a part of factor
payments. Therefore, these are included in the estimation of national income.

CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Q. 7. What causes increase in inventory stock?
Ans. Increase in inventory stock is caused by two factors:
(i) Unexpected Fall in Demand in the Current Year: Example: Producers may have expected
demand to the tune of 50,000 umbrellas but, owing to the failure of monsoon, only 10,000
umbrellas are sold during an year. Accordingly, 40,000 umbrellas are added to the existing
stock.
(ii) Expected Rise in Demand in the Near Future: Producers may expect a spurt (rise) in demand
(and therefore, increase in price) in the near future. Accordingly, they pile up stocks during
the current year.
Q.8. Export receipts are not a part of net factor income from abroad. Why?
Ans. This is because of two reasons:
(i) Exports refer to the purchase of domestically produced goods by the rest of the world.
Goods produced within the domestic territory of a country are to be treated as a part of
GDP.
(ii) Export receipts refer to revenue of the firms from the sale of its output. These are not the
receipts of factor incomes from abroad which are available in the form of rent, interest,
profit and wages.
Q. 9. Exports are just sales yielding revenue, not income. Comment.
Ans. It is true that exports are just sales and yield revenue, not income. Exports are just sales because
these are purchases of rest of the world from the domestic economy. Accordingly, exports yield
revenue (receipts from sales). These do not yield income. Because, income is in the form of rent,
interest, profit or wages. Exports do not yield any of these directly.
[Note: It is out of revenue that a firm distributes incomes to the owners of factors of production.]
Q. 10. Is net factor income from abroad zero in case exports = imports?
Ans. No. Net factor income from abroad is the difference between the factor income earned by
normal residents of a country from abroad and the factor income earned by non-residents in
our country. It has nothing to do with exports and imports.

• Precaution: Add only factor incomes, do not include transfer payments. Also, do not include

Q. 4. How do you distinguish between old-age persions and retirement pensions in the context of
estimation of national income?
Ans. Old-age pensions are unilateral payments or transfer payments. These are not included in the
estimation of national income. On the other hand, retirement pensions are like a deferred
wage. These are related to factor services rendered by the recipients prior to their retirement.
Accordingly, these are included in the estimation of national income,
Methods of Calculating National Income
Q. 5. Operating surplus does not arise in (i) subsistence sector, and (i) general government sector of
the economy. Why?
Ans. Operating surplus does not arise in the subsistence sector and in the general government sector
because of the following reasons:
(i) In the subsistence sector, production is meant only for subsistence of the producing families.
Production is not meant for sale in the market. There is no marketable surplus. Accordingly,
there is no operating surplus.
(ii) In the general government sector, production is meant only for collective consumption (or
consumption by the general public). Goods and services are produced not for sale in the
market, but for general welfare of the people.
Example: Services of law & order and defence are available to the people free of charge.
Accordingly, there is no operating surplus in the 'general government" sector.
Q. 6. How are dividends, corporate taxes and undistributed profits treated in national income?
Ans. (i) Dividends: These are included in the estimation of national income as these are a part of
factor payments.
(ii) Corporate Taxes: These are not included, as all taxes are transfer payments.
(iii) Undistributed Profits: These are retained earnings of the firms and are a part of factor
payments. Therefore, these are included in the estimation of national income.

boxes.title: CRITICAL QUESTIONS
boxes.text:
Q. 7. What causes increase in inventory stock?
Ans. Increase in inventory stock is caused by two factors:
(i) Unexpected Fall in Demand in the Current Year: Example: Producers may have expected
demand to the tune of 50,000 umbrellas but, owing to the failure of monsoon, only 10,000
umbrellas are sold during an year. Accordingly, 40,000 umbrellas are added to the existing
stock.
(ii) Expected Rise in Demand in the Near Future: Producers may expect a spurt (rise) in demand
(and therefore, increase in price) in the near future. Accordingly, they pile up stocks during
the current year.
Q.8. Export receipts are not a part of net factor income from abroad. Why?
Ans. This is because of two reasons:
(i) Exports refer to the purchase of domestically produced goods by the rest of the world.
Goods produced within the domestic territory of a country are to be treated as a part of
GDP.
(ii) Export receipts refer to revenue of the firms from the sale of its output. These are not the
receipts of factor incomes from abroad which are available in the form of rent, interest,
profit and wages.
Q. 9. Exports are just sales yielding revenue, not income. Comment.
Ans. It is true that exports are just sales and yield revenue, not income. Exports are just sales because
these are purchases of rest of the world from the domestic economy. Accordingly, exports yield
revenue (receipts from sales). These do not yield income. Because, income is in the form of rent,
interest, profit or wages. Exports do not yield any of these directly.
[Note: It is out of revenue that a firm distributes incomes to the owners of factors of production.]
Q. 10. Is net factor income from abroad zero in case exports = imports?
Ans. No. Net factor income from abroad is the difference between the factor income earned by
normal residents of a country from abroad and the factor income earned by non-residents in
our country. It has nothing to do with exports and imports.

title: Money
intro: Money is generally defined as a thing that is commonly accepted as a medium of exchange.

lessons.title: Money, barter and the evolution of money
lessons.body: Money is generally defined as a thing that is commonly accepted as a medium of exchange. Barter exchanges goods directly for goods. Its difficulties include lack of double coincidence of wants, lack of a common measure of value, difficulty storing wealth and difficulty making deferred payments. Money separates selling from buying: the seller need not want the precise good the buyer offers. Evolution moves through commodity money, metallic money, paper money and bank/credit money.

lessons.title: Fiat, fiduciary and legal-tender money
lessons.body: Fiat money is money issued by authority of the government. Fiduciary money is accepted on trust between payer and payee. Legal tender must be accepted in discharge of debts within the applicable legal conditions; a cheque depends on acceptance and is not legal tender. Full-bodied money has face value equal to intrinsic commodity value; credit money has face value greater than intrinsic value. Follow the textbook distinctions, not the everyday use of the word “cash”.

lessons.title: Primary and secondary functions of money
lessons.body: The primary functions are medium of exchange and measure of value (unit of account). Secondary functions are standard of deferred payments, store of value and transfer of value. Buying a book illustrates medium of exchange; quoting its price illustrates measure of value; paying a loan next year illustrates deferred payment; keeping purchasing power for later illustrates store of value. Inflation reduces the purchasing power stored in money.

lessons.title: Money supply and its components
lessons.body: Money supply is the stock of money held by the public at a particular point of time. Interbank deposits and money held by the government/banking system are excluded from money held by the public. M1 comprises currency with the public, demand deposits with commercial banks and other deposits with the RBI. Demand deposits are withdrawable on demand. A cheque transfers a deposit; it is not an additional independent stock of money.
lessons.formula: M1 = Currency with public + Demand deposits with banks + Other deposits with RBI

lessons.title: Ability Zone: broader measures and liquidity
lessons.body: The textbook also gives M2, M3 and M4 for reference. M2 adds post-office savings-bank deposits to M1. M3 adds net time deposits with commercial banks to M1 and is called aggregate monetary resources. M4 adds total post-office deposits, excluding National Savings Certificates, to M3. Liquidity means convertibility into cash: money is the most liquid asset. The textbook’s monetary-system notes discuss paper currency, limited/unlimited legal tender and the minimum reserve system; the original page is available to read exactly.

lessons.title: Why money solves barter’s difficulties
lessons.textbookHeading: 5.1.3 Barter System of Exchange · 5.3 Functions of Money
lessons.body: Lack of Double Coincidence of Wants: money is accepted as an intermediary, so you can sell to one person and buy from another. Lack of a Common Measure of Value: prices expressed in money make values comparable. Difficulty in Storing Wealth: money offers a convenient store, though inflation can erode it. Difficulty in Deferred Payments: future payments can be fixed in monetary units. Difficulty in Transfer of Value: purchasing power can be transferred without moving bulky goods. In theory answers, state the barter difficulty first and then the function that addresses it.

How Evolution of Money Led to Change in the Role of Money?
Evolution of money led to a significant change in the role of money in the economy.
Following observations highlight this point:
• Though initially invented as a medium of exchange, gradually money found its other uses as well.
People started using money as a store of value.
• Savings are no longer done by way of storage of goods. Money is used as an instrument of saving.
Further, money is used as a measure of value. People now express value of goods and services in
terms of money.
• Besides, money is serving as a standard for deferred payments (deferred payments are those
payments which are made sometimes in the future). Accordingly, money has acquired a wider
definition than merely a medium of exchange.
• Money is defined as an instrument that serves as a medium of exchange, store of value, measure
of value and standard for deferred payments. Briefly, it is said that 'money is what money does.

Store of Value
Standard for Deferred Payments
Goods and services can be exchanged because of money.
Price of different goods and services is determined in terms of money.
Money can be saved and stored for future use.
Money serves as a standard for deferred (future) payments.

Following are the principal drawbacks of barter system of exchange. It is with the introduction of
money that these drawbacks have been eliminated.
(1) Double Coincidence of Wants: Double coincidence of wants is a core characteristic of the
barter system of exchange.
• Double coincidence of wants implies that (at a point of time), the two individuals are in

wants.
• But, it is not so simple to find a person who wants your horse and at the same time has
a cow that you want to buy. Accordingly, under the barter system, exchange remained
extremely limited.
• With the emergence of money (as a medium of exchange), the problem of double
coincidence of wants has vanished. Money as a medium of exchange has separated the
acts of sale and purchase.

5.2 FORMS OF MONEY
Some important forms of money are described as under:
• Fiat money and fiduciary money, and
• Full bodied money and credit money.
5.2.1 Fiat Money and Fiduciary Money
•Fiat money refers to that money which is issued by order/authority of the government.
• It includes all notes and coins which the people in a country are legally bound to accept as a
medium of exchange.
• Fiduciary money is that money which is accepted as a medium of exchange because of the trust
between the payer and the payee.
Example:
Cheques are fiduciary money as these are accepted as a means of payment on the basis of
trust, not on the basis of any order of the government.
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Fiat Money/ Legal Tender Money
Legal tender is a coin or a banknote that is legally tenderable for discharge of debt or obligation.
It is divided into two parts:
(i) Limited Legal Tender
-Coins issued by the Government of India under the Coinage Act, 2011, are legal tender if they are not
defaced and weigh at least the prescribed minimum weight.
- Coins of one rupee or more are legal tender for amounts up to ? 1,000.
- Fifty paise coins are legal tender for amounts up to 710.

5.3 FUNCTIONS OF MONEY
Functions of money are placed in two categories:
• Primary functions, and
• Secondary (or Subsidiary) functions.
5.3.1 Primary Functions of Money
Money performs two primary functions, as under:
(1) Medium of Exchange: Money acts as a medium for the sale and purchase of goods and
services.
• In the absence of money, goods were exchanged for goods. This required double
coincidence of wants. Implying that, exchange was difficult, and therefore, limited.
• Introduction of money has separated the acts of sale and purchase: double coincidence of
wants is no longer a limitation.
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Significance of 'Medium of Exchange' Function of Money
• Exchange has become much simpler, and therefore, expanded considerably. Expansion of exchange
leads to expansion of value addition (or GDP growth).
• Exchange function of money has changed the nature of production activity. Production now is done
more for the market and less for self-consumption.
- Example: Farmers now produce wheat for sale in the market, not merely for self-consumption.
Accordingly, the level of production has substantially risen.
• Exchange function of money has separated the acts of sale and purchase. Accordingly, size of the
market has considerably expanded. This has also led to GDP growth.
(2) Measure of Value or Unit of value: Money serves as a measure of value or as a unit of
account, which implies that the value of each good or service is measured in the monetar
230
• Measurement of value was very difficult in the barter system: one good was valued in terms
of the other. There was no common unit of value. Introduction of money has removed this
difficulty. Now, each good is valued in terms of money.
• It is because of the existence of money as a common unit of value that we are now able to
construct consumer price index and wholesale price index. Consumer price index reflects
cost of living of the people. Wholesale price index shows the rate of inflation in the country.
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Significance of 'Unit of Value' Function of Money
• Common unit of value (in terms of money) has facilitated comparison of market value of different
assets.
-Accordingly, the market for sale and purchase of assets has considerably expanded. Expansion of
market has led to expansion of investment in the economy.
- Example: Investment in real estate has shown a significant growth over time, because the value of
different properties can be expressed in terms of a common unit of value.
• Common unit of value has facilitated the estimation of national income and related aggregates.
-Accordingly, it has become easy to assess performance of the economy over time. Without a common
unit of value, estimation of GDP (Index of Growth) was not possible.
5.3.2 Secondary or Subsidiary Functions of Money
Following three functions are secondary or subsidiary functions of money:
(1) Standard of Deferred Payments: Deferred payments refer to those payments which are
made sometimes in the future.
• Money has made deferred payments much easier than before. When we borrow money
from somebody, we have to return both the principal as well as interest amount, sometime
• Money is a convenient mode of these payments. It is difficult to make such payments in
terms of goods and services. Imagine that you have taken a loan from somebody in terms
of wheat. How difficult it is to return this loan in terms of wheat of the same quality?
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Significance of 'Standard of Deferred Payments' Function of Money
• This function of money has led to the emergence of 'financial market'-the market that deals in
borrowing and lending of money.
• Availability of credit through financial market has led to a multiple increase in consumption expenditure
as well as investment expenditure. Accordingly, there has been a multiple rise in the level of production
activity in the economy.
2) Store of Value: Store of value implies store of wealth.
• Storing wealth has become considerably easy with the introduction of money. Wealth can
be stored just in terms of paper titles like FDR (fixed deposit receipt.
• It was not convenient to store value in the barter system of exchange, Because, goods tenc
to wear-out or perish.

Introductory Macroeconomics
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Significance of Store of Value' Function of Money
• Stored wealth is a source of future investment, and investment is the principal determinant of GDP growt
• Convenient storage or wealth in terms of money has induced people to save more. saving is a virtue whe
converted into investment. However, it may be noted that idle saving leads to the deficiency of demand
It hinders the process of GDP growth.
(3) Transfer of Value: Money serves as a convenient mode of transfer of value (wealth). Money
value can be conveniently transferred (or can be e-transferred) to any part of the world.
• It is the transfer of value, which has led to the emergence of MINCS (Multinational
Corporations). Accordingly, the concept of global economy has come into existence.
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Significance of "Transfer of Value' Function of Money
• It has led to the emergence of Global Financial Market. Funds are easily available not only from
within the economy, but from across the borders as well.
-Accordingly, less developed countries find wider opportunities of investment through borrowing.
• Transfer of value has encouraged the growth of multinational corporations. This has raised the level of
global economic activity.
• Transfer of value has facilitated Direct Foreign Investment. This has accelerated the process of growth
in less developed economies.
• It has enhanced the mobility of capital across different regions of the country. Accordingly, balanced
regional growth has become an achievable target.
Static and Dynamic Functions
Functions of money are also viewed as: static functions and dynamic functions.
• Static Functions: Static functions of money refer to conventional functions of money.
- These basically include the primary and secondary functions of money: medium of exchange,
measure of value, store of value, transfer of value, and standard for deferred payments.
- Performing these functions, money helps in regulating the economic system.
• Dynamic Functions: Dynamic functions of money refer to those functions of money which impart
(a) stability to the economy, and (b) accelerate the pace of GDP growth.
- RBI (in India) tries to tackle the problem of inflation by lowering the supply of money.
- Further, it tries to tackle the problem of deflation (or economic slowdown) by increasing the supply
5.4 SUPPLY OF MONEY
5.4.1 Concept of Supply of Money
• Supply of money is a stock concept. It refers to total stock of money (of all types) held by the
people of a country at a point of time.
• It is important to note that the supply of money does not include:
• stock of money held by the government, and
• stock of money held by the banking system of a country.
232
• The stock of money held by the suppliers of money is never treated as a part of the supply of
money in the country as government and banking system of a country are the suppliers of money

(ii) deposits of the country's banking system with RBI.

5.4.3 Suppliers of Money or Who Supplies Money?
Following are the principal suppliers of money in an economy:
(1) Central Bank of the Country: The central bank of a country, like 'RBl' in India, 'The Federal
Reserve System in USA', and 'Bank of England' in UK.
• In India, RBI is the principal supplier of money. RBl issues currency on the basis of Minimum
Reserve System.
• Under this system, Reserve Bank maintains a minimum reserve of & 200 crore in the form
of gold and foreign securities. Of this reserve, value of the gold must be & 115 crore.
(2) Commercial Banks: Commercial banks are the second significant source of money supply.
Unlike the central bank, commercial banks do not have the authority of issuing currency nor
can they issue notes and coins. Yet, they are the suppliers of money as they create money by
way of demand deposits.
• These deposits serve as supply of money because these are chequeable deposits.
Money created by the commercial banks by way of demand deposits is called Bank
Money.
(3) The Government: Government is the third source of money supply in the country. In India,
the Ministry of Finance issues one rupee notes and coins of all denomination.

(i) the government of the country, and
(ii) the banking system of a country, including both the central bank (which is the note- issuing

Q. 11. Why are cash deposits of the government and of the commercial banks with the RBI no
treated as a part of money supply?
Ans. Because government and commercial banks are creators/suppliers of money. And, money held
by the creators/suppliers of money is never treated as a part of money supply.
0.12. What is meant by an ideal supply of money?
Ans. Ideal money supply is that amount of money supply which keeps the total purchasing power in
a state of balance with the supply of goods and services in the economy, so that the economy
does not slip into inflationary or deflationary situations.

• M Measurement
• My is also a broader concept of money supply compared to My. Besides all the components of
M, it also includes (net) time deposits (or fixed deposits/term deposits) of the people with the
commercial banks. Thus,
M3 = M, + Net Time Deposits with the Commercial Banks
• M Measurement
• My concept of money supply is still broader-it is broader than even M3. Besides all the

Aggregate Monetary Resources of the Country
If money supply in the country is measured using M3 measure, it is called 'aggregate monetary
resources' of the country.
'Narrow Money' and 'Broad Money' Concepts of Money Supply
• The distinction between narrow money and broad money is sometimes drawn with reference to the
measure used for estimating total money supply in the country.
•IfM, or M, measures are used, then it is known as 'narrow money' concept of money supply. If M3 or M4
measures are used, then it is known as "broad money' concept of money supply.
Indian Monetary System
• A monetary system refers to the form of money which circulates in the economy by way of order/authority
of the government. India is using paper currency. Accordingly, Indian monetary system is described as
a Paper Currency Standard.
Paper currency does not exclude the use of metal coins. Both metal coins and paper notes are credit
money in india. The only difference is that while coins are of small denomination, paper notes are of
large denomination.
Note Carefully
- Coins in India are limited legal tender.
- Paper notes in India are unlimited legal tender.
• It means that coins can be used to settle payments only of limited value; paper notes can be used to
settle payments of unlimited value.
What Governs Note Issuing in India?
• Note issuing in India is governed by Minimum Reserve System. The entire currency issued has the
backing of minimum gold reserves. Two points must be carefully understood in this context:
(i) Gold reserves are just the minimum reserves (2 115 crore). These are not proportionate to the
currency in circulation.
236
(i) Money with the people is entirely credit money. It cannot be converted into bullion-silver or gold
Money
by the issuing authority. Gold reserves are just a backing, not the stock to convert paper notes into gold.
The Concept of Liquidity
• Liquidity of an asset refers to its convertibility into money/cash. Faster an asset can be converted
into cash, more liquid it is. Obviously, money itself is the most liquid asset.
• Chequeable deposits/demand deposits are highly quid assets. Accordingly, we can state that M
includes only those components of money supply which are most liquid.
• Term deposits/time deposits/fixed deposits are not chequeable deposits. These cannot be withdrawi
by issuing a cheque. These deposits are, therefore, less liquid than the demand deposits.
Accordingly, M3 and M4 measures of money supply include such components of money supply which
are less liquid.
Power Points [Summary of the Chapter]
• Money is anything which is commonly accepted as a medium of exchange.
• It has been invented to overcome the difficulties of barter system of exchange.
• Barter System of Exchange is the system in which commodities are exchanged for commodities.
• This is also called commodity for commodity exchange economy or 'C-C economy.
• Drawbacks:
) It requires double coincidence of wants which is hard to find.
(i) It lacks a common unit of exchange.
(i) It lacks the system of future payments or deferred payments.
(iv) It lacks the system of storage and transfer of value.
• Forms of Money
• Fiat Money is that money which is issued by order (authority) of the government.
• Fiduciary Money is that money which is accepted as a medium of exchange because of the trust
between the payer and the payee.
• Full Bodied Money: Money value = Commodity value of money.
• Credit Money: Money value of coins and notes > Commodity value of coins and notes.
• Functions of Money
• Primary Functions:
- It serves as a medium of exchange.
- It is a standard unit of value.
• Secondary Functions:
- It is a standard of deferred payments.
- It is a store of value.
- It facilitates transfer of value.
* Supply of Money is a stock concept. It refers to stock of money available with the public/people at
a point of time.
• Stock of Money with the government and the banking system of the country is not considered
as a part of money supply.
• Components of Money Supply:
Currency with Public + Demand Deposits with Commercial Banks + Other Deposits with the
Reserve Bank.

How Evolution of Money Led to Change in the Role of Money?
Evolution of money led to a significant change in the role of money in the economy.
Following observations highlight this point:
• Though initially invented as a medium of exchange, gradually money found its other uses as well.
People started using money as a store of value.
• Savings are no longer done by way of storage of goods. Money is used as an instrument of saving.
Further, money is used as a measure of value. People now express value of goods and services in
terms of money.
• Besides, money is serving as a standard for deferred payments (deferred payments are those
payments which are made sometimes in the future). Accordingly, money has acquired a wider
definition than merely a medium of exchange.
• Money is defined as an instrument that serves as a medium of exchange, store of value, measure
of value and standard for deferred payments. Briefly, it is said that 'money is what money does.

Significance of 'Medium of Exchange' Function of Money
• Exchange has become much simpler, and therefore, expanded considerably. Expansion of exchange
leads to expansion of value addition (or GDP growth).
• Exchange function of money has changed the nature of production activity. Production now is done
more for the market and less for self-consumption.
- Example: Farmers now produce wheat for sale in the market, not merely for self-consumption.
Accordingly, the level of production has substantially risen.
• Exchange function of money has separated the acts of sale and purchase. Accordingly, size of the
market has considerably expanded. This has also led to GDP growth.
(2) Measure of Value or Unit of value: Money serves as a measure of value or as a unit of
account, which implies that the value of each good or service is measured in the monetar
230
• Measurement of value was very difficult in the barter system: one good was valued in terms
of the other. There was no common unit of value. Introduction of money has removed this
difficulty. Now, each good is valued in terms of money.
• It is because of the existence of money as a common unit of value that we are now able to
construct consumer price index and wholesale price index. Consumer price index reflects
cost of living of the people. Wholesale price index shows the rate of inflation in the country.

boxes.title: CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
boxes.text:
Significance of 'Unit of Value' Function of Money
• Common unit of value (in terms of money) has facilitated comparison of market value of different
assets.
-Accordingly, the market for sale and purchase of assets has considerably expanded. Expansion of
market has led to expansion of investment in the economy.
- Example: Investment in real estate has shown a significant growth over time, because the value of
different properties can be expressed in terms of a common unit of value.
• Common unit of value has facilitated the estimation of national income and related aggregates.
-Accordingly, it has become easy to assess performance of the economy over time. Without a common
unit of value, estimation of GDP (Index of Growth) was not possible.
5.3.2 Secondary or Subsidiary Functions of Money
Following three functions are secondary or subsidiary functions of money:
(1) Standard of Deferred Payments: Deferred payments refer to those payments which are
made sometimes in the future.
• Money has made deferred payments much easier than before. When we borrow money
from somebody, we have to return both the principal as well as interest amount, sometime
• Money is a convenient mode of these payments. It is difficult to make such payments in
terms of goods and services. Imagine that you have taken a loan from somebody in terms
of wheat. How difficult it is to return this loan in terms of wheat of the same quality?

boxes.title: CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
boxes.text:
Significance of 'Standard of Deferred Payments' Function of Money
• This function of money has led to the emergence of 'financial market'-the market that deals in
borrowing and lending of money.
• Availability of credit through financial market has led to a multiple increase in consumption expenditure
as well as investment expenditure. Accordingly, there has been a multiple rise in the level of production
activity in the economy.
2) Store of Value: Store of value implies store of wealth.
• Storing wealth has become considerably easy with the introduction of money. Wealth can
be stored just in terms of paper titles like FDR (fixed deposit receipt.
• It was not convenient to store value in the barter system of exchange, Because, goods tenc
to wear-out or perish.

boxes.title: CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
boxes.text:
Significance of Store of Value' Function of Money
• Stored wealth is a source of future investment, and investment is the principal determinant of GDP growt
• Convenient storage or wealth in terms of money has induced people to save more. saving is a virtue whe
converted into investment. However, it may be noted that idle saving leads to the deficiency of demand
It hinders the process of GDP growth.
(3) Transfer of Value: Money serves as a convenient mode of transfer of value (wealth). Money
value can be conveniently transferred (or can be e-transferred) to any part of the world.
• It is the transfer of value, which has led to the emergence of MINCS (Multinational
Corporations). Accordingly, the concept of global economy has come into existence.

boxes.title: CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
boxes.text:
Significance of "Transfer of Value' Function of Money
• It has led to the emergence of Global Financial Market. Funds are easily available not only from
within the economy, but from across the borders as well.
-Accordingly, less developed countries find wider opportunities of investment through borrowing.
• Transfer of value has encouraged the growth of multinational corporations. This has raised the level of
global economic activity.
• Transfer of value has facilitated Direct Foreign Investment. This has accelerated the process of growth
in less developed economies.
• It has enhanced the mobility of capital across different regions of the country. Accordingly, balanced
regional growth has become an achievable target.
Static and Dynamic Functions
Functions of money are also viewed as: static functions and dynamic functions.
• Static Functions: Static functions of money refer to conventional functions of money.
- These basically include the primary and secondary functions of money: medium of exchange,
measure of value, store of value, transfer of value, and standard for deferred payments.
- Performing these functions, money helps in regulating the economic system.
• Dynamic Functions: Dynamic functions of money refer to those functions of money which impart
(a) stability to the economy, and (b) accelerate the pace of GDP growth.
- RBI (in India) tries to tackle the problem of inflation by lowering the supply of money.
- Further, it tries to tackle the problem of deflation (or economic slowdown) by increasing the supply

boxes.title: CRITICAL QUESTIONS
boxes.text:
Q.9. Who are the producers of money?
Ans. Producers of money refer to suppliers of money. They include:
(i) the government of the country, and
(ii) the banking system of a country, including both the central bank (which is the note- issuing
authority) and the commercial banks (who add to the supply of money through demand
deposits).
9.10. State the principal components of money supply.
Ans. The principal components of money supply are:
(i) Currency (notes + coins) held by the public.
(i) Demand deposits of the people with the commercial banks, and
(i) Other deposits (demand deposits with RBl of domestic and foreign institutions other than
of the government of the country and commercial banks within the country.
Q. 11. Why are cash deposits of the government and of the commercial banks with the RBI no
treated as a part of money supply?
Ans. Because government and commercial banks are creators/suppliers of money. And, money held
by the creators/suppliers of money is never treated as a part of money supply.
0.12. What is meant by an ideal supply of money?
Ans. Ideal money supply is that amount of money supply which keeps the total purchasing power in
a state of balance with the supply of goods and services in the economy, so that the economy
does not slip into inflationary or deflationary situations.

Indian Monetary System
• A monetary system refers to the form of money which circulates in the economy by way of order/authority
of the government. India is using paper currency. Accordingly, Indian monetary system is described as
a Paper Currency Standard.
Paper currency does not exclude the use of metal coins. Both metal coins and paper notes are credit
money in india. The only difference is that while coins are of small denomination, paper notes are of
large denomination.
Note Carefully
- Coins in India are limited legal tender.
- Paper notes in India are unlimited legal tender.
• It means that coins can be used to settle payments only of limited value; paper notes can be used to
settle payments of unlimited value.

(i) Gold reserves are just the minimum reserves (2 115 crore). These are not proportionate to the
currency in circulation.

The Concept of Liquidity
• Liquidity of an asset refers to its convertibility into money/cash. Faster an asset can be converted
into cash, more liquid it is. Obviously, money itself is the most liquid asset.
• Chequeable deposits/demand deposits are highly quid assets. Accordingly, we can state that M
includes only those components of money supply which are most liquid.
• Term deposits/time deposits/fixed deposits are not chequeable deposits. These cannot be withdrawi
by issuing a cheque. These deposits are, therefore, less liquid than the demand deposits.
Accordingly, M3 and M4 measures of money supply include such components of money supply which
are less liquid.

boxes.title: Power Points [Summary of the Chapter]
boxes.text:
• Money is anything which is commonly accepted as a medium of exchange.
• It has been invented to overcome the difficulties of barter system of exchange.
• Barter System of Exchange is the system in which commodities are exchanged for commodities.
• This is also called commodity for commodity exchange economy or 'C-C economy.
• Drawbacks:
) It requires double coincidence of wants which is hard to find.
(i) It lacks a common unit of exchange.
(i) It lacks the system of future payments or deferred payments.
(iv) It lacks the system of storage and transfer of value.
• Forms of Money
• Fiat Money is that money which is issued by order (authority) of the government.
• Fiduciary Money is that money which is accepted as a medium of exchange because of the trust
between the payer and the payee.
• Full Bodied Money: Money value = Commodity value of money.
• Credit Money: Money value of coins and notes > Commodity value of coins and notes.
• Functions of Money
• Primary Functions:
- It serves as a medium of exchange.
- It is a standard unit of value.
• Secondary Functions:
- It is a standard of deferred payments.
- It is a store of value.
- It facilitates transfer of value.
* Supply of Money is a stock concept. It refers to stock of money available with the public/people at
a point of time.
• Stock of Money with the government and the banking system of the country is not considered
as a part of money supply.
• Components of Money Supply:
Currency with Public + Demand Deposits with Commercial Banks + Other Deposits with the
Reserve Bank.

title: Banking
intro: Commercial banks accept deposits and advance loans with the objective of earning profit.

lessons.title: Commercial banks and their functions
lessons.body: Commercial banks accept deposits and advance loans with the objective of earning profit. Deposits include current, savings and fixed deposits. Primary functions are accepting deposits and lending; other functions include agency services and general-utility services. Banks mobilise saving and create demand deposits through lending. A central bank is the apex institution regulating the monetary and financial system; its objective is growth with stability rather than commercial profit.

lessons.title: Credit creation: follow every round
lessons.body: Suppose an initial cash deposit of 1,000 enters the banking system and the reserve ratio is 20%. The first bank keeps 200 and lends 800. If 800 is redeposited, the next bank keeps 160 and lends 640. Repeated lending and redepositing expand total deposits to 5,000. These results assume no cash leakage, no excess reserves and loans redeposited in the banking system. Total deposits include the initial deposit; additional credit excludes it.
lessons.formula:
Deposit multiplier = 1 ÷ Reserve ratio
Total deposits = Initial deposit ÷ Reserve ratio
Additional credit = Total deposits − Initial deposit
lessons.textbookHeading: 6.2 MONEY CREATION BY THE COMMERCIAL BANKS

lessons.title: Central bank: seven functions
lessons.body: The textbook lists issuer of currency, banker to the government, bankers’ bank and supervisor, lender of last resort, custodian of foreign exchange, clearing-house function and control of credit. As government banker it holds accounts, receives money, makes payments and manages borrowing. As bankers’ bank it holds bank reserves and supports banks. Clearing settles interbank claims. Lender of last resort provides emergency assistance when normal sources cannot meet a bank’s needs.

lessons.title: Quantitative instruments: rates and open market operations
lessons.body: Bank rate, repo rate and reverse repo rate influence the cost and placement of funds. The textbook distinguishes bank-rate lending without collateral from repo lending against securities under a repurchase agreement. Raising lending rates tends to raise borrowing cost and reduce credit demand; lowering them works in the opposite direction. RBI sales of securities absorb liquidity and reduce credit creation; RBI purchases release liquidity and increase it. These are textbook mechanisms, not a claim about today’s policy rates.

lessons.title: Reserve ratios and qualitative instruments
lessons.body: CRR is the percentage of deposits banks must keep with the RBI. SLR requires banks to maintain prescribed liquid assets such as cash, gold and approved securities. Higher reserve requirements constrain lending; lower requirements release lending capacity. Margin requirement is the difference between collateral value and loan value. Higher margins reduce permitted loans. Rationing fixes credit quotas, while moral suasion uses persuasion and pressure to influence bank lending. Quantitative instruments affect overall credit; qualitative instruments target its allocation.

lessons.title: Ability Zone: when monetary tools succeed
lessons.body: Repo-rate policy depends on banks’ reliance on RBI loans, responsiveness of credit demand, the wider structure of interest rates and availability of non-bank funds. Open market operations require a functioning securities market and an effective link between reserve changes and lending. Explaining a policy requires the transmission chain: policy change → bank funds or borrowing cost → credit → expenditure → aggregate demand.
lessons.textbookHeading: ABILITY ZONE · Success of Repo Rate · Success of Open Market Operations

lessons.title: Issuer of currency and banker to government
lessons.body: Issuer of Currency: the central bank has the principal note-issuing authority; in India, the ₹1 note and coins are issued by the Government of India. Centralised issue promotes uniformity and control. Banker to Government: the RBI keeps government deposits, receives payments, makes disbursements, advances funds within the applicable arrangements and manages public debt. Financial adviser is a related role. Distinguish issuing authority from circulation: government-issued coins enter circulation through the monetary system.

lessons.title: Bankers’ bank, lender of last resort and clearing house
lessons.body: Bankers’ Bank and Supervisory Role: commercial banks maintain required cash balances with the central bank, which regulates their functioning. Lender of Last Resort: the central bank offers financial accommodation in emergencies when other sources are unavailable. Clearing House: it settles interbank claims by adjusting banks’ accounts and facilitates fund transfers. Custodian of Foreign Exchange: it manages the country’s foreign-exchange reserves and can intervene in the exchange market. Control of Credit: it regulates the cost and availability of credit to support growth with stability.

6.1 COMMERCIAL BANKS
Commercial banks are an important component of banking system of a country. Let us first understand
what a commercial bank means.
Meaning of Commercial Bank
* A commercial bank is that financial institution which accepts deposits from the people and gives
loans for the purpose of consumption or investment.
• Besides, commercial banks perform various other functions such as credit creation, transfer of
funds, agency jobs and general services.
• According to Indian Banking Companies Act, "Banking company is one which transacts the
business of banking which means the accepting (for the purpose of lending or investment) of
deposits of money from the public repayable on demand or otherwise and withdrawable by
cheque, draft, order or otherwise."

• Unlike the central bank, the commercial banks do not have the authority of issuing currency: they
cannot issue notes or coins. Yet, they are the suppliers of money as they create money by way of
demand deposits.

banks create money?

• Primary deposits are cash deposits with the commercial banks by the people. These are a part of total

• Secondary deposits are those deposits which arise on account of loans by the banks to the people.
These are also a part of total demand deposits of the banks.

• Demand deposits serving as money supply is called bank money. This is money created by the

• Success of repo rate policy as an instrument of credit control depends on the following factors:

> If commercial banks have their own surplus funds which they can utilise during periods of
high credit needs, their dependence on the central bank is reduced.
• Degree of Sensitivity of Bank's Demand for Funds from the Central Bank:

variations in repo rate. In such situations, repo rate policy may not be a big success.
• Structure of Interest Rates in the Money Market:
› Ifnon-banking financial institutions in the market do not vary their interest rates in accordance
with what the central bank expects from the commercial banks, the repo rate policy may not
succeed.
• Overall Supply of Funds in the Market:
> Repo rate policy may not be a success if non-banking sources of funds are more popular
than the banking sources.
Success of Open Market Operations as an Instrument of Credit Control
• Success of open market operations as an instrument of credit control depends on the following factors:
• Existence of Securities Market:
›There must be a well organised and well functioning market for the sale and purchase of
securities. In the absence of it, open market operations would be of little significance as an
instrument of monetary policy.
• Excess Reserves with the Banks:
• If commercial banks have healthy excess reserves as Vault Cash' they need not buy
securities. This is the standard practice in developed countries like USA. Accordingly, open
market operations fail to be a successful instrument of credit control.

Primary and Secondary Deposits
• Primary deposits are cash deposits with the commercial banks by the people. These are a part of total
demand deposits of the banks.
• Secondary deposits are those deposits which arise on account of loans by the banks to the people.
These are also a part of total demand deposits of the banks.
• Important to note it is, that while primary deposits indicate savings of the depositors with the banks,
secondary deposits indicate borrowings of the depositors from the banks. Secondary deposits are also
called Derivative Deposits.
Total Demand Deposits of the People with the Commercial Banks
= Primary Deposits of the Commercial Banks + Secondary/Derivative Deposits of the
Commercial Banks
• Total demand deposits with the banks are many times more than the cash reserves of the

• Success of repo rate policy as an instrument of credit control depends on the following factors:

• Structure of Interest Rates in the Money Market:

succeed.
• Overall Supply of Funds in the Market:
> Repo rate policy may not be a success if non-banking sources of funds are more popular
than the banking sources.
Success of Open Market Operations as an Instrument of Credit Control

• Existence of Securities Market:

instrument of monetary policy.
• Excess Reserves with the Banks:

securities. This is the standard practice in developed countries like USA. Accordingly, open
market operations fail to be a successful instrument of credit control.

title: Aggregate Demand, Aggregate Supply and Related Concepts
intro: Aggregate demand is the sum total of demand for all goods and services during an accounting year, measured as planned expenditure.

lessons.title: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply
lessons.body: Aggregate demand is the sum total of demand for all goods and services during an accounting year, measured as planned expenditure. In a two-sector economy AD = C + I; a closed economy with government adds G; an open economy adds X − M. Aggregate supply refers to production planned by producers. In the textbook’s short-run model with constant prices and spare capacity, AS is identified with income/output and represented by the 45° line.
lessons.formula:
AD = C + I + G + (X − M)
AS = Y = C + S
lessons.textbookHeading: 7.1 CONCEPT OF AD · 7.2 COMPONENTS OF AD · 7.3 CONCEPT OF AS

lessons.title: Consumption function: autonomous and induced consumption
lessons.body: Consumption function is the functional relationship between consumption and income. Autonomous consumption is consumption when income is zero; induced consumption is the part that varies with income. In C = C̄ + bY, the vertical intercept is C̄ and the slope b is MPC. Consumption rises with income, but normally by less than the rise in income. A change in income moves along a given function; a change in autonomous consumption shifts it.
lessons.formula:
C = C̄ + bY
MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY
Induced consumption = bY

lessons.title: APC and MPC: totals versus increments
lessons.body: Average propensity to consume is total consumption divided by total income; marginal propensity to consume is additional consumption divided by additional income. APC may exceed one when consumption exceeds income. MPC is the slope of the consumption curve; APC is not. With positive autonomous consumption and constant MPC below one, APC falls as income rises. At zero income APC is undefined.
lessons.formula:
APC = C ÷ Y
MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY

lessons.title: Saving function and the break-even point
lessons.body: Saving is income not consumed. Derive S by subtracting the entire consumption function from Y. The saving function has a negative intercept equal to autonomous consumption and a slope equal to MPS. At break-even income C = Y and S = 0: APC is one and APS is zero. Below it saving is negative; above it saving is positive. Break-even is not necessarily equilibrium, because equilibrium also depends on investment.
lessons.formula:
S = Y − C = −C̄ + (1 − b)Y
Break-even income = C̄ ÷ (1 − b)

lessons.title: APS, MPS and the two identities
lessons.body: Average propensity to save is S/Y; marginal propensity to save is ΔS/ΔY. APS can be negative when households dissave. MPS is the slope of the saving function. Since income is split between consumption and saving, APC + APS = 1 and MPC + MPS = 1. Do not confuse ΔS (change in saving) with AS (aggregate supply): similar letters represent different concepts.
lessons.formula:
APS = S ÷ Y; MPS = ΔS ÷ ΔY
APC + APS = 1; MPC + MPS = 1
lessons.textbookHeading: APS vs. MPS · Relationship between Propensity to Consume and Propensity to Save

lessons.title: Investment and deriving one function from the other
lessons.body: In the simple model autonomous investment is independent of income, so its curve is horizontal. Induced investment responds to changes in income or activity. The expected profitability of investment and rate of interest influence investment decisions. To obtain C from S, use C = Y − S; to obtain S from C, use S = Y − C. The two slopes add to one and their vertical intercepts have equal magnitudes with opposite signs.
lessons.textbookHeading: INVESTMENT · ABILITY ZONE: Derivation of C-function from S-function

lessons.title: Ranges of APC, MPC, APS and MPS
lessons.textbookHeading: Comparative Table of APC, MPC, APS and MPS · Critical Questions
lessons.body: APC can exceed one when C exceeds Y; it equals one at break-even and is below one when saving is positive. APS is negative when saving is negative, zero at break-even and positive when saving is positive; with positive consumption it remains below one. MPC and MPS range from zero to one in the textbook model and add to one. At the endpoints, MPC = 1 implies MPS = 0 and all additional income is consumed; MPC = 0 implies MPS = 1 and all additional income is saved. Do not infer a marginal ratio from a single total-income observation.

7.4 CONSUMPTION FUNCTION
7.4.1 Concept of Consumption Function
• Household consumption expenditure (C) is an important component of aggregate demand in
the economy. It is directly related to the level of income (Y). Higher Y leads to higher C, and
vice versa.
•The functional relationship (or the algebraic relationship) between CandY is called Consumption
Function. It reveals the behaviour of household consumption expenditure with respect to the
level of income in the economy.
• Studying the behaviour of C with respect to Y, the economists have identified the following points
as of central significance:
• There is always some minimum level of C, even when Y = 0. This is called autonomous
consumption. This leads to negative saving (-S).

title: Short Run Equilibrium Output
intro: The textbook’s short run assumes constant technology and a given capital stock; changes in employment change output.

lessons.title: Short run and equilibrium output
lessons.body: The textbook’s short run assumes constant technology and a given capital stock; changes in employment change output. Equilibrium output is the level where intended production equals intended expenditure. Producers have no unplanned change in inventories and no incentive to change output. In the two-sector economy Y = C + I and Y = C + S, so the same equilibrium condition can be written S = I.
lessons.formula:
Y = AD = C + I
C + S = C + I ⇒ S = I
Y* = (C̄ + I) ÷ (1 − MPC)
lessons.textbookHeading: 8.1 CONCEPT OF SHORT RUN · 8.2 CONCEPT OF EQUILIBRIUM OUTPUT

lessons.title: How inventories restore equilibrium
lessons.body: When AD is below AS, goods remain unsold and actual inventories exceed desired inventories. Producers cut output and employment until planned saving equals planned investment. When AD exceeds AS, inventories fall unexpectedly and producers expand output, provided spare capacity exists. The direction is easy to reverse by mistake: excess supply causes inventory accumulation; excess demand causes inventory depletion.

lessons.title: Ex-ante versus ex-post saving and investment
lessons.body: Ex-ante means planned; ex-post means realised. Planned saving and planned investment need not be equal away from equilibrium. Actual saving and actual investment are equal by accounting identity because realised investment includes unintended inventory changes. Equilibrium requires equality of planned S and planned I, not merely the ex-post identity.

lessons.title: Effective demand and underemployment equilibrium
lessons.body: Effective demand is aggregate demand at the equilibrium level of income/output. Equilibrium can occur below full employment: firms’ production plans can match spending plans while workers and productive capacity remain idle. An increase in autonomous expenditure shifts AD upward and raises equilibrium output in the model with spare capacity; a fall lowers it.

lessons.title: Investment multiplier: size and derivation
lessons.body: Investment multiplier is the ratio of change in income to change in investment. Starting with ΔY = ΔC + ΔI and ΔC = MPC × ΔY gives ΔY(1 − MPC) = ΔI. Higher MPC means more income is respent, so the multiplier is larger. Higher MPS means more income leaks into saving, so the multiplier is smaller. With MPC zero, k = 1; as MPC approaches one, k becomes very large.
lessons.formula:
k = ΔY ÷ ΔI = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPS
ΔY = k × ΔI

lessons.title: Multiplier mechanism, assumptions and reverse operation
lessons.body: An investment injection is someone’s income. They consume a fraction, which becomes someone else’s income; successive rounds generate ΔI, MPC × ΔI, MPC² × ΔI and so on. Saving reduces each next round. The simple multiplier assumes constant MPC, available spare capacity, constant prices, and no additional leakages such as imports or taxes. A fall in investment works in reverse, producing a multiplied fall in income. The final increase in saving equals the initial increase in investment.

lessons.title: Break-even income versus equilibrium income
lessons.body: Break-even Income: consumption equals income, so saving is zero; use C = Y. Equilibrium Income: planned output equals planned expenditure, so saving equals investment; use Y = C + I or S = I. With positive autonomous investment and positive MPS, equilibrium income exceeds break-even income. The two coincide only when autonomous investment is zero in the simple model. If you are asked for dissaving at zero income, solve for autonomous consumption and report saving as its negative.
lessons.formula:
Break-even Y = C̄/MPS
Equilibrium Y = (C̄ + I)/MPS

pages.text:
Introductory Macroeconomics
8.1 CONCEPT OF SHORT RUN
Understanding the Concept of Short Run
• Output is determined exclusively by the level of emproyment in the economy. "Higher level of
to remain constant.
employment leads to higher level of output, and vice versa." Technology remaining constant, there
is one-to-one relationship between output and employment. Thus, if employment is doubled,
output will also be doubled.
• In other words, the level of employment in the economy measures the level of output (GDP) in
the economy. Accordingly, output cannot increase once there is full employment in the economy.
8.2 CONCEPT OF EQUILIBRIUM OUTPUT (GDP)
Two Approaches of Equilibrium
(i) AS = AD Approach
• Equilibrium output (also called equilibrium GDP or equilibrium income) refers to that level of
output in the economy where:
AD
[Aggregate Supply = Aggregate Demand]
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Why is there an equilibrium in the economy when AS = AD?
• Because in such a situation, intended production in the economy is equal to intended purchase in the
economy. The producers do not suffer:
- The burden of unwanted supplies (or unsold stocks), or
- The loss of unfulfilled demand (due to lack of stocks).
• When AS = AD, actual stocks with the producers = desired stocks with the producers.
We have already learnt in the previous chapter that:
• AS refers to the desired level of output in the economy. It is the level of GDP that the producers
wish to produce (or plan to produce) during an accounting year (also called ex-ante AS).
• AD, on the other hand, refers to the level of GDP that the buyers wish to buy during an accountin
year (also called ex-ante AD).
• The equilibrium GDP means that level of GDP where what the producers wish to produce (or

What happens if AS < AD?

Situation:
When AS is less than AD (AS < AD), supply of goods and services in the economy tends

with the demand) causes loss to the producers.

AS would increase to become equal to AD. This is how AS converges with AD. Thus,
equilibrium is restored through a change in output or a change in Y.
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Three Basic Assumptions related to Equilibrium GDP
Three basic assumptions of the Keynesian theory must be noted:
• Short Period Analysis: Equilibrium GDP according to Keynesian theory is discussed only with reference
to short period of time.
• Two Sector Closed Economy: Initially, Keynes discusses the theory of equilibrium GDP in the context
of a two sector closed economy. Accordingly, AD = C+ I (when only household sector and producer
sector are considered).
• AS is Perfectly Elastic: Keynes assumes that AS is perfectly elastic.
- It means that we are studying an economy in which there is an 'excess capacity': production capacity
is lying idle or there is unemployment of resources. So that, whenever there is a rise in AD, there is a
corresponding rise in AS (as excess capacity begins to be utilised).
- Thus, AS always aligns itself with AD, without causing any change in the price level.

• We have seen how additional investment (AI) causes additional output (AY) in the economy.

in output/income and increase in investment.

boxes.text:
Three Basic Assumptions related to Equilibrium GDP
Three basic assumptions of the Keynesian theory must be noted:
• Short Period Analysis: Equilibrium GDP according to Keynesian theory is discussed only with reference
to short period of time.
• Two Sector Closed Economy: Initially, Keynes discusses the theory of equilibrium GDP in the context
of a two sector closed economy. Accordingly, AD = C+ I (when only household sector and producer
sector are considered).
• AS is Perfectly Elastic: Keynes assumes that AS is perfectly elastic.
- It means that we are studying an economy in which there is an 'excess capacity': production capacity
is lying idle or there is unemployment of resources. So that, whenever there is a rise in AD, there is a
corresponding rise in AS (as excess capacity begins to be utilised).
- Thus, AS always aligns itself with AD, without causing any change in the price level.

lessons.title: Full employment and unemployment
lessons.body: Full employment means those able and willing to work at the existing wage obtain work. Voluntary unemployment reflects unwillingness to work at the existing wage; involuntary unemployment means willing workers cannot find jobs. The textbook also distinguishes natural unemployment: frictional unemployment during job transitions and structural unemployment caused by changing industries, skills or production techniques. Underemployment equilibrium has AD = AS with unutilised capacity.

lessons.title: Deficient demand and deflationary gap
lessons.body: Deficient demand occurs when aggregate demand is less than the aggregate supply corresponding to full employment. The deflationary gap is the shortfall of AD from the level required to maintain full employment; measure it vertically at full-employment output. It reduces output and employment and creates involuntary unemployment. The gap in expenditure is not the same as the shortfall in equilibrium income: the multiplier links the two.
lessons.formula:
Deflationary gap = Yf − AD at Yf
Required increase in autonomous expenditure = (Yf − Y*) ÷ k

lessons.title: Excess demand and inflationary gap
lessons.body: Excess demand occurs when AD exceeds the demand required to sustain full employment. The inflationary gap is the excess of AD over full-employment AS, measured at Yf. Once resources are fully employed, real output cannot expand in the simple model; excess spending raises the general price level. A calculated equilibrium above Yf is a signal of inflationary pressure, not evidence that the economy can actually produce beyond its capacity.
lessons.formula: Inflationary gap = AD at Yf − Yf

lessons.title: Fiscal measures: expenditure, taxation and borrowing
lessons.body: To correct deficient demand, raise government expenditure, reduce taxes, reduce public borrowing and increase borrowing from the central bank, following the textbook framework. These measures raise spending power or public expenditure. For excess demand, reverse the direction. Explain the chain: lower taxes → higher disposable income → more consumption → higher AD. Borrowing from the public can withdraw purchasing power; borrowing from the central bank can expand it.

lessons.title: Monetary measures: cost and availability of credit
lessons.body: For deficient demand, lower bank/repo/reverse-repo rates, lower CRR and SLR, buy securities, lower margins, relax credit rationing and encourage lending. For excess demand, raise rates and reserve requirements, sell securities, raise margins and restrict lending. Monetary policy is the central bank’s policy; fiscal policy is the government’s revenue and expenditure policy. Always connect the instrument to credit and then to aggregate demand.

Q.2. How does propensity to consume affect AD-function?
Ans. Increase in the propensity to consume causes an upward shift in the AD-function (through an
upward shift in the C-function). On the other hand, decrease in the propensity to consume
causes a downward shift in AD-function (through a downward shift in C-function).
Q. 3. According to Keynes, price level rises only after full employment. Why?
Ans. Price level does not rise before full employment, because AS is assumed to be perfectly elastic.
Prior to full employment, AS tends to rise proportionate to any rise in AD. Accordingly, price level
remains constant. But after full employment is reached, AS stops rising in response to a rise in
AD. Accordingly, price level tends to rise.

Introductory Macroeconomics
Let us understand how these policies are used to combat inflationary gap (related to excess demand
and deflationary gap (related to deficient demand).
9.4.1 Fiscal Policy (Fiscal Measures)
• Fiscal policy refers to revenue and expenalture policy of the government. It is also calle
Budgetary Policy of the government.
• It focuses on stability of the economy by correcting the situations or excess demand (inflationar
gap) and deficient demand (deflationary gap).
Components of Fiscal Policy and the Way these are Used
Following are the principal components of fiscal policy. Along with each component, we are
describing the way it is used to correct the situations of excess and deficient demand.
(1) Government Expenditure: It is the principal component (or principal instrument) of fiscal
policy. The government of a country incurs various types of expenditure, mainly:
(i) Expenditure on public works programmes such as the construction of roads, dams,
bridges, etc.
(ii) Expenditure on education and public welfare programmes.
(iii) Expenditure on the defence of the country and the maintenance of law & order.
(iv) Expenditure on various types of subsidies to the producers with a view to encourage
production.
• It is by changing any or all types of expenditure that the government seeks to correct
the situations of excess demand or deficient demand in the economy. When there is
excess demand, government expenditure is reduced, and when there is deficient demand,
government expenditure is increased.
• A rise in government expenditure acts as an "injection' into the circular flow of income in
the economy. It is required when liquidity needs to be released to combat deflation.
• Likewise, a cut in government expenditure acts like a 'withdrawal' from the circular flow of
income in the economy. It is required when liquidity needs to be soaked to combat inflation.
(2) Taxes: Taxes are a compulsory payment made to government by the household.
• By increasing the tax burden on the households, the government reduces their disposable
income. Accordingly, AD is reduced or excess demand is managed.
• On the other hand, by lowering the tax burden, the government increases disposable
income of the households. Accordingly, AD is raised and deficient demand is managed.
(3) Public Borrowing/Public Debt: By borrowing from the public, the government creates public
debt.
• In a situation of deficient demand (or when AD needs to be increased), the government
reduces its borrowing from the public. So that people are left with greater liquidity (or cash
balances) and aggregate expenditure remains high.
• On the other hand, when there is a situation of excess demand (or when AD needs to be
reduced, the government steps up public borrowing by offering attractive rate of interest.
This reduces liquidity with the people. Accordingly, aggregate expenditure also reduces
and excess demand is managed.

Q. 4. What fiscal measures would you recommend to correct deficient demand?
Ans. Following fiscal measures are recommended to correct deficient demand:
i The govern secred step up its expenditure [on a public works programmes,
(b) education and public welfate, (c) subsidies to the producers, and (d) defence and
law & order]. Higher government expenditure acts like an injection into the circular flow of
income in the economy.
i) The government should reduce tax burden on the households, so that they are left with
greater cash balances. Higher cash balances with the people lead to higher level of AD.
(i) The government should raise more funds from the RBI so that there is a greater flow of
liquidity in the economy. Higher liquidity implies higher level of AD.
(iv) The government should plan a cut in public borrowing, so that, people are left with greater
liquidity (or cash balances). Greater cash balances implies higher AD.
Briefly, deficient demand is corrected when the government steps up its own expenditure and
ensures that cash balances with the people are raised.

9.4.2 Monetary Policy (Monetary Measures)
• Monetary policy refer to that policy which deals with the control of liquidity or flow of credit in
the market with a view to managing inflationary or deflationary gaps in the economy.
• We have already described the components of monetary policy and the way these are used to
correct the situations of excess demand (inflationary gap) and deficient demand (deflationary gap)
in the economy in chapter 6. Here, we present a brief summary of that description. Application of
monetary instruments to correct excess demand and deficient demand is discussed separately.
as under:
Application of Monetary Instruments to Correctthe Situation of Excess Demand
• Bank rate and repo rate are raised by the RBI. As a follow-up action, market rate of interest Is
raised by the commercial banks. Cost of borrowing rises. It lowers the demand for credit leas
to a cut in consumption and investment expenditure in the economy. Implying a cut in AD, as

• In a situation of deficient demand, AD needs to be raised. The RBl pursues cheap money policy.
Availability of credit is raised and cost of credit is lowered. It is achieved by using the montary
instruments exactly the opposite way these are used in a situation of excess demand or inflationary

Avoiding repetition, we may state that (for the correction of deficient demand), the availability of
credit is raised and the cost of credit is lowered through the following montary actions by the RBI:

creation of credit.

for the creation of credit.
• CRR is lowered to increase the supply of credit.

• Margin requirement is lowered to raise the availability of credit.
• Moral pressure is built on the commercial banks to be liberal in lending.

Discretionary and Non-discretionary Fiscal Instruments
• Non-discretionary fiscal instruments refer to those fiscal instruments which start operating automatically
on their own. These are also called auto-stabilisers.
On the other hand, discretionary instruments are those instruments which are planned by the government
to correct the situations of excess and deficient demand. We have already discussed in detail various
discretionary instruments. As regards non-discretionary instruments, some illustrations may prove to be
useful.
• A rise in AD automatically raises tax revenue and a fall in AD automatically decreases tax
revenue. Accordingly, taxation acts as an auto-stabiliser in the economy, It lowers AD when
excess demand is to be corrected. And, it raises AD when deficient demand is to be corrected.
• Grants and subsidies are other examples of non-discretionary fiscal instruments or
auto-stabilisers in the economy. During periods ofboom (when excess AD needs to be corrected),
grants and subsidies come down on their own, causing a cut in government expenditure and
thereby a cut in AD. During periods of depression, on the other hand, grants and subsidies tend
to rise. It implies a rise in government expenditure and therefore, a rise in AD, as desired to
correct deficient demand during depression.

Q.2. How does propensity to consume affect AD-function?
Ans. Increase in the propensity to consume causes an upward shift in the AD-function (through an
upward shift in the C-function). On the other hand, decrease in the propensity to consume
causes a downward shift in AD-function (through a downward shift in C-function).
Q. 3. According to Keynes, price level rises only after full employment. Why?
Ans. Price level does not rise before full employment, because AS is assumed to be perfectly elastic.
Prior to full employment, AS tends to rise proportionate to any rise in AD. Accordingly, price level
remains constant. But after full employment is reached, AS stops rising in response to a rise in
AD. Accordingly, price level tends to rise.
