Ans. Following fiscal measures are recommended to correct deficient demand:
i The govern secred step up its expenditure [on a public works programmes,
(b) education and public welfate, (c) subsidies to the producers, and (d) defence and
law & order]. Higher government expenditure acts like an injection into the circular flow of
income in the economy.
i) The government should reduce tax burden on the households, so that they are left with
greater cash balances. Higher cash balances with the people lead to higher level of AD.
(i) The government should raise more funds from the RBI so that there is a greater flow of
liquidity in the economy. Higher liquidity implies higher level of AD.

liquidity (or cash balances). Greater cash balances implies higher AD.
Briefly, deficient demand is corrected when the government steps up its own expenditure and
ensures that cash balances with the people are raised.

lessons.title: Government budget and its objectives
lessons.body: Government budget is a statement of expected receipts and expected expenditure of the government for the coming financial year, revealing its budgetary policy. Objectives include GDP growth, allocation of resources, redistribution of income and wealth, economic stability, management of public enterprises and employment generation. Public infrastructure can encourage private investment; progressive taxation and social spending can reduce inequality. Fiscal discipline means managing public finances responsibly to avoid unsustainable deficits and debt.

lessons.title: Revenue receipts versus capital receipts
lessons.body: Revenue receipts neither create a liability nor reduce assets. They include tax revenue and non-tax revenue such as fees, fines, interest, profits/dividends and grants. Capital receipts create a liability or reduce assets: borrowing creates liabilities, while loan recovery and disinvestment reduce assets. Do not classify a receipt by size or regularity alone; use the liability/asset test.

lessons.title: Direct taxes, indirect taxes and non-tax revenue
lessons.body: Direct taxes have impact and incidence on the same person, such as income tax and corporation tax. Indirect taxes allow the burden to be shifted, such as GST. A fee is a payment for a specific government service; a fine penalises an offence. A tax is compulsory and does not promise a direct equivalent service. Progressive taxes take a larger proportion as income rises; proportional taxes keep the same proportion; regressive burdens fall relatively more heavily on lower incomes.

lessons.title: Revenue expenditure versus capital expenditure
lessons.body: Revenue expenditure neither creates assets nor reduces liabilities. Salaries, pensions, subsidies and interest payments are examples. Capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities: construction of a highway, purchase of equipment, lending by government and repayment of loan principal. Repayment of principal is capital expenditure; interest is revenue expenditure. Grants to states remain revenue expenditure for the granting government even if the recipient uses them to build assets, following the textbook convention.

lessons.title: Revenue deficit, fiscal deficit and primary deficit
lessons.body: Revenue deficit is the excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings; it measures borrowing requirements. Primary deficit deducts interest payments from fiscal deficit and indicates the current borrowing requirement excluding past-debt interest. A zero revenue deficit does not guarantee zero fiscal deficit. A zero primary deficit means borrowing covers interest payments.
lessons.formula:
Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts
Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − Revenue receipts − Non-debt capital receipts
Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments
lessons.textbookHeading: 10.4 BUDGET DEFICIT: REVENUE DEFICIT, FISCAL DEFICIT AND PRIMARY DEFICIT

lessons.title: Implications, balanced and unbalanced budgets
lessons.body: A revenue deficit indicates government dissaving: borrowing may finance current consumption rather than asset creation. Fiscal deficits may raise debt and interest burdens and crowd out private borrowing; financing expenditure can also support demand and productive capacity, depending on its use. A balanced budget has receipts equal to expenditure; a surplus budget has receipts above expenditure and can restrain inflation; a deficit budget can support demand in recession. Consider both the size and composition of expenditure.

lessons.title: Ability Zone: public, private, common and club goods
lessons.body: Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, such as national defence. Private goods are rival and excludable. Common goods are rival but non-excludable, such as fish in an open pond. Club goods are excludable but non-rival until congestion, such as a subscription service. Rivalry means one person’s use reduces availability to others; excludability means users can be denied access. Public expenditure supports infrastructure, redistribution, stability and an investment-friendly environment.
lessons.textbookHeading: ABILITY ZONE · Public Goods, Private Goods, Common Goods and Club Goods

lessons.title: Budget objectives: the headings to reproduce
lessons.body: GDP Growth: create infrastructure and induce private investment through suitable incentives. Allocation of Resources: influence production through taxes, subsidies and public provision. Provision of Public Goods: provide collective services that markets may undersupply. Redistribution of Income and Wealth: use progressive taxation and welfare spending. Balanced Regional Growth: direct infrastructure and incentives to less-developed regions. Employment Opportunities: expand activity and labour demand. Economic Stability: raise spending during deficient demand and restrain it during excess demand. Select and explain the number of objectives requested, using these headings.

lessons.title: Free-rider problem
lessons.body: A free rider enjoys the benefits of goods and services without contributing the full or partial cost of providing them. Non-excludability makes it difficult to withhold benefits from non-payers. Private providers may be unable to collect enough revenue to cover costs, so the market can fail to provide a needed public good. National defence and street lighting illustrate why public provision can be necessary.

lessons.title: Tax rates and tax burden are different
lessons.textbookHeading: ABILITY ZONE · Progressive and Regressive Nature of Taxation is Different from Progressive and Regressive Rates of Taxation
lessons.body: Progressive Rate: the tax rate rises with income. Regressive Rate: the tax rate falls with income. Proportionate Rate: the tax rate stays constant as income changes. Progressive Nature: the real burden is greater on the rich. Regressive Nature: the real burden is greater on the poor. The textbook stresses that a proportionate tax can still have a regressive real burden. When answering, specify whether you mean the numerical rate or the economic burden.

lessons.title: Does a balanced budget leave AD unchanged?
lessons.textbookHeading: ABILITY ZONE · Does Balanced Budget Leave Aggregate Demand Unaffected in the Economy?
lessons.body: No. Equal tax collection and government expenditure do not necessarily have equal first-round effects on AD. Government expenditure enters AD in full; a tax increase reduces disposable income, and consumption falls by MPC times the tax rise. If G and taxes each rise by ₹100 and MPC is 0.5, expenditure raises AD by ₹100 while the initial consumption loss is ₹50, giving a net initial rise of ₹50. Under the simple lump-sum-tax model, later rounds imply a balanced-budget multiplier of one. Distinguish the initial AD change from the final income change.
lessons.formula:
Initial ΔAD = ΔG − MPC × ΔT
If ΔG = ΔT: initial ΔAD = (1 − MPC)ΔG

10.1 CONCEPT OF GOVERNMENT BUDGET
Meaning and Features of Government Budget
• February-1 is a well known date in India when the Finance Minister presents annual budget of
the government for its approval by the parliament.
• The budget unfolds:
* the financial performance of the government over the past one year, and
• the financial programmes and policies of the government for the next one year.
• It includes an estimate of government receipts and government expenditure for the upcoming
• Asregards financial performance of the government, it is more like a description of what happened
during the past one year. Focus is placed largely on the other part of the budget describing
programmes and policies (and estimates of receipts and expenditure) of the government for the
next one year.
• The programmes and policies of the government (as presented in the budget) are known as
"Budgetary Policy' of the government, or 'Fiscal Policy' of the government. It has the following
aspects:

• It is by managing the expected revenue and expected expenditure that the government reveals
its fiscal policy (budgetary policy), focusing on growth and stability of the economy.
Thus, government budget is a statement of expected receipts and expected expenditure of the
government (for the financial year to come that reveals budgetary policy of the government to
achieve the twin objective of growth with stability.
10.2 OBJECTIVES OF GOVERNMENT BUDGET **
Following is a brief description of some principal objectives of government budget (with special
reference to the Indian economy):
(1) GDP Growth: GDP growth is the central objective of government budgetary policy. It is
achieved in two ways:
• By expanding public expenditure particularly on the creation of economic and social
infrastructure.
• By inducing private investment expenditure (through tax rebates and subsidies).
(2) Allocation of Resources: Private enterprises will always desire to allocate resources to
those areas of production where profits are high. However, it is possible that such areas of
production (like production of alcohol) may not promote social welfare.
• Through its budgetary policy, the government of a country directs the allocation of resources

(i) Provision of Public Goods: Supply and demand forces in a market economy do not allow
enough production of public goods. These are those goods which satisfy collective needs
• Law & order and defence of the country are important examples of public goods. It is through
budgetary allocation of funds that these goods are sufficiently provided to the people.
Check Ability Zone for details on how public goods are different from other goods!
(4) Redistribution of Income and Wealth: Taxation and subsidies are important components a
government budget. These are used to correct the distribution of income and wealth.
• Taxes are imposed on the rich and subsidies are offered to the poor. Accordingly disposable
income of the rich is reduced, while the disposable income of the poor is increased.
• Free LPG connection to the BPL population is an important example of subsidy to the poor.
f) Balanced Regional Growth: The budgetary policy places priority on the development of
backward regions in the country. This is achieved through liberal tax laws for the backward
regions.
• Establishment of SEZ (special economic zones) in the backward regions through liberal tax
laws may be cited as an example.
(6) Employment Generation: Budgetary policy focuses on the generation of employment
opportunities through investment in public enterprises.
• Budgetary provisions are made for schemes like MGNREGA offering employment to poorer
sections of the society.
(7) Economic Stability: Revenue and expenditure policies of the government are used as fiscal
instruments to minimise the inflationary and deflationary swings in the economy.
• Inflation is corrected through higher taxation and lower government expenditure.
• Deflation is managed through lower taxation and higher government expenditure.
Lily the government tries to manage its revenue and expenditure in such a way that the
(I growth is accelerated, inflationary and deflationary pressures are eliminated, and inequality is
educed. This imparts stability to the process of growth.

Q.2. How does the government's budgetary policy strike a balance between profit maximisation by
private enterprises and the promotion of social welfare?
Ans. The government's budgetary policy strikes a balance between private profit maximisation and
promotion of social welfare through the following ways:
(i) The government promotes the production of socially useful goods (like khadi) by offering
tax-rebates and subsidies to the producers. Simultaneously taxes (like GST) are lowered to
promote sales of such goods.
Example: Under the Zero Defect Zero Effect (ZED) Scheme, the Government of India provides
upto 80% subsidy to Mini, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs).
(i) On the other hand, socially harmful goods (like cigarettes and alcohol are highly taxed to
discourage their production as well as consumption.
(i) Profit maximisation is supported through high budgetary allocations to the construction of
SEZ (Special Economic Zones), offering banking and transport facilities to the producers.
(iv) Also, subsidies are offered on the purchase of 'capital goods', like tractors by the farmers so
that their cost of production is minimised and profits are maximised.
0. 3. In what ways does the government budget contribute to economic stability, particularly during
periods of inflation and deflation?
Ans.
(i) Inflation is managed by decreasing government expenditure, so that AD is reduced. Also,
taxes are raised to minimise disposable income of the people. When disposable income
reduces, expenditure (AD) also reduces.
(ii) Deflation is managed by raising government expenditure, so that AD is raised. Taxes are
lowered to raise disposable income, so that AD is boosted. Business houses are offered
'bail-out' packages so that their scale of production is not impaired.

Details of both these components are discussed as under:
10.3.1 Budget Receipts
• Budget receipts refer to estimated money receipts of the government from all sources during
the fiscal year.
• Broadly, the budget receipts are classified as:

(b) Capital Receipts.

(a) Progressive and Regressive Taxes: Taxes are classited as progressive and regressive
depending on the real burden of taxation. Details are as under:
• Progressive Tax: A tax is said to be progressive when the rate of tax increases with an
increase in income. So that, the real burden of the taxis more on the rich and less on the poc
Suppose there is a tax system where the tax rate is 10% for annual income betwee
* 8 to * 12 lakh. It is say 15% for annual income between 12 to ‹ 16 lakh, and so o
Thus, tax rate increases as the level of income increases.
• Regressive Tax: A tax is said to be regressive when it causes a greater real burden on the
poor than the rich.
If a person with 71,00,000 as his monthly income pays 10% income tax (or pays 1000),
he still has a balance of 90,000 per month.
But if a person with ‹ 5,000 as his monthly income has to pay 10% income tax or pays
7 500), it might mean a cut in his essential consumption leading to poor diet and
therefore, poor health.
Thus, a constant rate of taxation on the rich and the poor is a regressive tax, as it causes
a greater real burden on the poor than the rich.
(b) Value Added Tax or VAT and Specific Taxes: Depending upon tax base, taxes can be classified as:
• Value Added Tax or VAT: Value added tax is an indirect tax which is imposed on 'Value
Added' at the various stages of production.
> Value added refers to the difference between value of output and value of intermediate
consumption. It is imposed at each stage of production. GST is an important form of value
added tax.
• Specific Tax: When a tax is levied on a commodity on the basis of its units, size or weight,
it is called the specific tax.
Example:
Excise Duty on Petrol and Diesel: Levied per litre of fuel sold. Tax on Packaged Goods:
Charged per unit or per weight (e.g., R 5 per 500 ml of soft drink).
(c) Direct and Indirect Taxes: Taxes are classified as direct and indirect depending on their final
burden.
• Direct Tax: A direct tax is the one the final burden of which is borne by the person on
whom it is imposed.
Example:
Income tax. It is imposed on the income of a person and he himself bears its burden.
burden of this tax cannot be shifted to any other person. Corporation tax, gift tax, wea
tax, are other examples of direct tax.
• Indirect Tax: An indirect tax is the one whose initial burden or impact is on one person bu
he succeeds in shifting the burden to another persons.

(ii) Non-tax Receipts
Non-tax receipts are those receipts which arise from sources other than taxes. Some of the non-tax
receipts are as follows:
(a) Fees: A fee is a payment to the government for the services that it renders to the people.
Examples:
Land registration fees, birth and death registration fees, passport fees, court fees, etc.
It is to be noted that fee is not a payment (price) for commercial service. It is a payment for
administrative and judicial services provided to the people.
(b) Fines: Fines are those payments which are made by the law breakers to the govemment.
These are economic punishments for breaking laws. The aim is not to earn revenue, but to
make people respectful to the laws.
(c) Escheat: Escheat refers to that income of the state which arises out of the property left by
the people without a legal heir. There are no claimants of such property. The government
makes revenue out of it.
(d) Special Assessment: Special assessment is that payment which is made by the owners of those
properties whose value has appreciated due to developmental activities of the government.
Example:
When as a result of construction of roads or provision of sewerage system or construction
of drains, etc., value of the neighbouring property or its rental value appreciates, then a
part of the developmental expenditure is recovered from the owners of such property by
way of special assessment.

10.3.1 (b) Capital Receipts
Capital receipts are those money receipts of the government which show the following two
characteristics:
(i) These receipts create a liability for the government.
Example:
Loans by the government are a liability. These are to be paid back. These are, therefore,
the capital receipts of the government.
(ii) These receipts cause reduction in assets of the government.
Example:
Money received by the government by selling its shares (say of Air India) would cause
reduction in assets of the government. These are, therefore, to be treated as capital receipts.
In short, capital receipts are those money receipts of the government which either create a liability
for the government or cause a reduction in its assets.

(i) Recovery of Loans: The central government offers loans to the state governments to cope

Accordingly, these are classified as capital receipts.
(i) Borrowings and Other Liabilities: While lending creates assets, borrowing creates liability.
Accordingly, borrowings are to be treated as capital receipts. It may be noted that the

• The Reserve Bank of India, and
• The rest of the world.
(il) Other Receipts: These include items like 'disinvestment". It is the opposite of investment.
Disinvestment occurs when the government sells off its shares of public sector enterprises
to private sector.
• It involves transfer of ownership of public sector enterprises to the private entrepreneurs,
leading to privatisation. Money received through disinvestment is treated as capital receipt
because it causes reduction in assets of the government.

10.3.2 Budget Expenditure
• Budget expenditure refers to estimated expenditure of the government during the fiscal year.
• Like budget receipts, budget expenditure of the government is broadly classified as:
(a) Revenue Expenditure and
(b) Capital Expenditure.
Following are the details:
10.3.2 (a) Revenue Expenditure
Revenue expenditure of the government is that expenditure which shows the following two
characteristics:
(i) It does not create any asset for the government.
Example:
Expenditure by the government on old-age pensions, salaries and scholarships are to be
treated as revenue expenditure. Because this does not lead to any type of asset formation.
(i) It does not cause any reduction in liability of the government.
Example:
Expenditure by way of grants to the state government to cope with natural calamities (like
floods and earthquakes) does not reduce financial liability of the central government in any
manner. Accordingly, this is to be treated as revenue expenditure.

In short, revenue expenditure refers to estimated expenditure of the government in a fiscal year
which does not create assets or causes a reduction in liabilities.

Important Convention regarding Grants
As a matter of convention, all grants given by the centre to the state governments and the governments
of Union territories) are treated as revenue expenditure, even when some grants may result in the creation
of assets.
10.3.2 (b) Capital Expenditure
Capital expenditure of the government is that expenditure which shows the following two
characteristics:
(i) It creates assets for the government.
Example:
Equity (or shares) of the domestic or multinational corporations purchased by the government
creates assets for the government. Accordingly, this is to be treated as capital expenditure.
(i) It causes reduction in liabilities of the government.
Example:
Repayment of loans certainly reduces liability of the government. Accordingly, this is to be F
treated as capital expenditure.
In short, capital expenditure refers to the estimated expenditure of the government in a fiscal year
which creates assets or causes a reduction in liabilities.

10.5 BALANCED AND UNBALANCED BUDGET
10.5.1 Concept of Balanced Budget-Its Merits and Demerits
Abalanced budget is that budget in which government receipts are equal to government expenditure.
Balanced Budget:
Government Receipts = Government Expenditure
Merits and Demerits of Balanced Budget
Merits
• The government does not indulge in wasteful expenditure.
• A balanced budget ensures financial stability. It signals fiscal discipline in the economy.
However, during the general depression of 1930's, the policy of balanced budget was severely
criticised. It was then that the following shortcomings of a balanced budget were highlighted.
Shortcomings or Demerits
• Balanced budget does not offer any solution to the problem of unemployment. Particularly.
when unemployment is linked with the lack of AD. It happened in most European Countries
during 1930's.
• Balanced budget is not conducive to growth in less developed countries. Kick start of growth
in these economies depends on a big-push of investment expenditure by the government.
This often leads to deficit budget.
10.5.2 Concept of Unbalanced Budget-Its Types, Merits and Demerits
An unbalanced budget is that budget in which receipts and expenditures of the government are not
equal. This may be a situation of:
(i) Surplus Budget, or
idget.

Introductory Macroeconomics
(i) Surplus Budget
This is a budget in which government receipts are greater than government expenditures.
Surplus Budget:
Estimated Government Receipts > Estimated Government Expenditures
Merits and Demerits of Surplus Budget
• Surplus budget (when, receipts > expenditures) is desired when the economy is battling inflation
due to excess AD.
• Surplus budget plugs the inflationary gap by lowering the level of AD. AD is lowered on account of
(a) rise in revenue collection by the government, and
(b) fall in government expenditure.
Demerits
• As surplus budget tends to lower the level of AD in the economy, it is not desired during periods
of depression.
• If surplus budget policy is constantly pursued by the government, AD may reduce to a level that
causes unemployment in the economy. The economy may be driven into a low level equilibrium
Lap.
(il) Deficit Budget
This is a budget in which government expenditures are greater than government receipts.
Deficit Budget:
Estimated Government Expenditures > Estimated Government Receipts
Keynes and other modern economists stress significance of deficit budget, highlighting its merits.
Merits and Demerits of Deficit Budget
Merits
• Keynes recommends deficit budget as a key instrument to correct the state of depression.
• According to him, depression is that phase of economic activity when the level of investment
is low owing to the low level of AD. Consequently, planned output is much lower than the full
employment level of output. Unemployment becomes a national problem. Deficit budget raises
the level of AD in two ways:
(a) Directly by way of high government expenditure, and
(b) Indirectly by inducing greater (investment and consumption) expenditure by the people.
Demerits
• Deficit budget is not desired during periods of inflation. It is a period when the AD exceeds AS
at full employment.
• Deficit budget in such situations (when AS cannot increase) would further increase the guir
between AD and AS. Consequently, inflationary gap would rise and wage-price spiral (when
wages increase with prices and prices increase with wages) may set in.

Significance or Importance of Public Expenditure
(with reference to the Indian Economy)
Following observations highlight the significance of public expenditure with reference to the Indian
economy:
(1) Public expenditure accelerates the pace of GDP growth. Higher rate of GOP growth is achieved
through
> investment expenditure in public sector enterprises,
› capital grants by the government for the purchase of capital equipment,
› subsidies for the purchase of inputs, and
› purchase of farm output at the minimum support price.
(i) Public expenditure promotes equality in the distribution of income and wealth. This is achieved by
offering old-age pensions, as well as by providing free food, education, and health services to the
Below Poverty Line Population.
ii) Public expenditure plays a significant role in restoring economic stability. Particularly, when the
economy is battling economic recession. The government expenditure (consumption expenditure
as well as investment expenditure) raises the level of AD. Only when AD is raised that the vicious
circle of economic recession is broken.
(iv) Public expenditure generates investment-friendly environment in the economy. The government
spends money on infrastructural development. It constructs roads, dams, bridges. It introduces
faster and convenient means of transportation. Such facilities promote inducement to investment.
• Briefly, public expenditure is indispensable in any welfare state like India. It not only promotes GDP
growth, but also promotes social welfare.

*Rivalry: Use by one limits the availability of the good for the other.

Public Goods vs. Private Goods
• Public Goods
• Public goods are the goods which are meant for collective use by all sections of the
society, Example: Law and order, defence and public administration. These goods have two
characteristics:
(i) Non-rivalrous: These goods are non-rivalrous in the sense that the use of a public good by one
individual does not reduce its availability for the other.
Example: Parks, national defence, when used by one individual are not reduced for the other.
483

Introductory Macroeconomics
(i) Non-excludability: These goods are non-exclusive in the sense that the use of a public good by
those individuals who pay for it does not exclude others from using it who do not pay for it.
Example: Street light may be a paid utility service. But those who do not pay cannot be excluded
from the use/benefit of it. These goods, therefore, have the problem of free-riders: even those
who do not pay for them continue to use them.
• Private Goods
• The opposite of a public good is a private good. A private good is rivalrous and excludable.
Personal car of an individual is an example of a private good.
• It does not carry the characteristics of
) non-rivalrous, and
(ii) non-excludability.
• Because, this particular car when purchased by me reduces the availability of cars by one unit,
and secondly, since I have paid for it, others obviously have no right to use it.
Free Rider Problem
A free rider is a person who enjoys the benefits of goods and services without contributing to the full cost
or partial cost of providing them. Consumers can take advantage of public goods without contributing
sufficiently to their creation. This is called the free rider problem.
• The free rider problem is usually more acute in the case of public goods. The free rider problem exists
when people enjoy the benefits of government provided goods independent of whether they pay for
them. If too many consumers decide to 'free ride', private costs exceed private benefits and the incentive
to provide the good or service through the market disappears. The market, thus, fails to provide a good
or service for which there is a need.
Progressive and Regressive Nature of Taxation is Different from
Progressive and Regressive Rates of Taxation
• Progressive Rate: The rate of taxation increases with increase in income.
• Regressive Rate: The rate of taxation decreases with increase in income.
• Proportionate Rate: The rate of taxation remains constant with increase or decrease in income.
• Progressive Tax: A tax which (in terms of nature/effect) causes greater real burden on the rich compared
to the poor.
• Regressive Tax: A tax which (in terms of nature/effect) causes greater real burden on the poor compared
to the rich. This implies that even a proportionate tax is a regressive tax.

Land registration fees, birth and death registration fees, passport fees, court fees, etc.
It is to be noted that fee is not a payment (price) for commercial service. It is a payment for
administrative and judicial services provided to the people.
(b) Fines: Fines are those payments which are made by the law breakers to the govemment.
These are economic punishments for breaking laws. The aim is not to earn revenue, but to
make people respectful to the laws.
(c) Escheat: Escheat refers to that income of the state which arises out of the property left by
the people without a legal heir. There are no claimants of such property. The government
makes revenue out of it.
(d) Special Assessment: Special assessment is that payment which is made by the owners of those
properties whose value has appreciated due to developmental activities of the government.
Example:
When as a result of construction of roads or provision of sewerage system or construction
of drains, etc., value of the neighbouring property or its rental value appreciates, then a
part of the developmental expenditure is recovered from the owners of such property by
way of special assessment.

Capital receipts are those money receipts of the government which show the following two
characteristics:
(i) These receipts create a liability for the government.
Example:
Loans by the government are a liability. These are to be paid back. These are, therefore,
the capital receipts of the government.
(ii) These receipts cause reduction in assets of the government.

Money received by the government by selling its shares (say of Air India) would cause
reduction in assets of the government. These are, therefore, to be treated as capital receipts.
In short, capital receipts are those money receipts of the government which either create a liability
for the government or cause a reduction in its assets.

(i) Recovery of Loans: The central government offers loans to the state governments to cope

(i) Borrowings and Other Liabilities: While lending creates assets, borrowing creates liability.

Significance or Importance of Public Expenditure
(with reference to the Indian Economy)
Following observations highlight the significance of public expenditure with reference to the Indian
economy:
(1) Public expenditure accelerates the pace of GDP growth. Higher rate of GOP growth is achieved
through
> investment expenditure in public sector enterprises,
› capital grants by the government for the purchase of capital equipment,
› subsidies for the purchase of inputs, and
› purchase of farm output at the minimum support price.
(i) Public expenditure promotes equality in the distribution of income and wealth. This is achieved by
offering old-age pensions, as well as by providing free food, education, and health services to the
Below Poverty Line Population.
ii) Public expenditure plays a significant role in restoring economic stability. Particularly, when the
economy is battling economic recession. The government expenditure (consumption expenditure
as well as investment expenditure) raises the level of AD. Only when AD is raised that the vicious
circle of economic recession is broken.
(iv) Public expenditure generates investment-friendly environment in the economy. The government
spends money on infrastructural development. It constructs roads, dams, bridges. It introduces
faster and convenient means of transportation. Such facilities promote inducement to investment.
• Briefly, public expenditure is indispensable in any welfare state like India. It not only promotes GDP
growth, but also promotes social welfare.

title: Foreign Exchange Rate
intro: Foreign exchange refers to foreign currency.

lessons.title: Foreign exchange and the quotation convention
lessons.body: Foreign exchange refers to foreign currency. Foreign exchange rate is the price paid in domestic currency for a unit of foreign currency. Throughout these lessons, quote the rate as ₹ per US dollar. A rise from ₹80/$ to ₹84/$ means the rupee buys fewer dollars and has depreciated; a fall to ₹76/$ means rupee appreciation. Always identify which currency is in the numerator before describing a movement.
lessons.textbookHeading: 11.1 FOREIGN EXCHANGE AND FOREIGN EXCHANGE RATE

lessons.title: Demand, supply and flexible exchange-rate determination
lessons.body: Flexible exchange rate is determined by demand and supply in the foreign exchange market. Demand for foreign exchange comes from imports, overseas investment, foreign travel, loan repayment, income payments, grants and speculation. Supply comes from exports, foreign investment, inward loans, tourism receipts, income receipts, grants and remittances. With ₹/$ on the vertical axis, demand slopes downward and supply upward; their intersection is the equilibrium rate. A higher exchange rate makes foreign goods costlier in rupees and normally reduces import-related foreign-exchange demand.

lessons.title: Movements versus shifts, appreciation versus depreciation
lessons.body: A change in the exchange rate causes movement along a given demand or supply curve. A change in imports, investment preferences, income or foreign demand shifts a curve. Greater demand for dollars shifts demand right, raising ₹/$ and depreciating the rupee. Greater supply of dollars shifts supply right, lowering ₹/$ and appreciating the rupee. Depreciation can make exports cheaper for foreigners and imports costlier for residents; actual quantity responses depend on demand conditions.
lessons.textbookHeading: Appreciation and Depreciation of Domestic Currency

lessons.title: Fixed rate, devaluation and revaluation
lessons.body: Fixed exchange rate is set and maintained by the monetary authority. An official rise in ₹/$ is devaluation of the rupee; an official fall is revaluation. Depreciation/appreciation describe market-driven changes under a flexible system. To defend a fixed rate when demand for dollars exceeds supply, the authority sells foreign currency from reserves; when dollar supply exceeds demand it buys foreign currency. An overvalued domestic currency tends to create excess demand for foreign currency at the official rate.

lessons.title: Managed floating and merits/demerits
lessons.body: Managed floating combines market determination with occasional central-bank intervention to limit undesirable movements; the textbook also calls it dirty floating. Fixed rates reduce exchange uncertainty and can support trade but require reserves and may misallocate resources. Flexible rates need less reserve defence and adjust through markets but create uncertainty and exposure to external shocks. The original comparison covers the full list of merits and demerits.

lessons.title: Foreign exchange market: transfer, credit and hedging
lessons.body: The foreign exchange market is the market for national currencies. The transfer function moves purchasing power between countries. The credit function supports trade through financing arrangements. Hedging reduces exchange-rate risk. Spot transactions exchange currency for current delivery; forward transactions agree today on a rate for delivery at a future date. A forward contract fixes an exchange rate; it does not guarantee that the future spot rate will equal that rate.

lessons.title: Fixed versus flexible rates: named merits and demerits
lessons.textbookHeading: 11.4 MERITS AND DEMERITS OF FIXED AND FLEXIBLE EXCHANGE RATE
lessons.body: Fixed Rate—Merits: market stability and mobility of capital; growth of international trade; stable macroeconomic policies; devaluation as a policy tool; a check on inflation. Fixed Rate—Demerits: large reserve requirements; inefficient allocation of resources; limited forex market; discouraged venture capital; possible divergence from equilibrium. Flexible Rate—Merits: fewer reserves required for rate defence; market allocation of resources; larger forex market; international mobility of liquidity; support for venture capital. Flexible Rate—Demerits: weak-currency marginalisation; market uncertainty; difficulty maintaining stable monetary policy; difficulty with bilateral trade agreements; external shocks. These are the textbook’s headings: explain the relevant mechanism instead of only listing them.

Less developed countries often devalue their currency: domestic currency is made cheaper in relation to

) Devaluation (implying a planned fall in the value of the domestic currency) is expected to raise the

(i) A fall in the value of domestic currency induces private foreign investment. Because, for every
dollar, the investors are going to get more rupees, after devaluation. This is expected to promote
GDP growth.
Gold Standard System of Exchange Rate -
An Old Variant of Fixed Exchange Rate System
• Gold standard system of exchange rate is an old variant of fixed exchange rate system.
• According to this system (prevalent in most countries prior to 1920s), gold was taken as the
common unit of parity between currencies of different countries. Each country was to define
value of its currency in terms of gold. Accordingly, value of one currency in terms of the other
currency was fixed considering gold value of each currency.
Example:
If UK € (Pound) = 4 g of gold, and US $ (Dollar) = 2 g of gold, then 1 UKE = 2 USS.
Exchange rate or exchange ratio between UK E and US $ = 1: 2. Two US dollars would
exchange for 1 UK pound.
• This system of exchange was also known as Mint Par Value of Exchange or Mint Parity. Mint value
of a currency implied gold value of that currency.

, Even when exchange rate is determined by the forces of supply and demand, at times the Central

• Managed floating is a system of floating exchange rate in which there is occasional
intervention by the central bank to influence the float or manage the float. It is also called
Dirty Floating'.
How does the Central Bank exercise its influence on the 'Float' or Market Exchange Rate?
• Itis through the sale and purchase of foreign currency in the international money market. When
the exchange rate (say of US $) needs to be reduced, the central bank releases the supply of
US $ in the foreign exchange market.
If 1 US dollar is worth & 75, and the RBI sells US dollars, the price may drop to 7 72, causing

Example:

• On the other hand, when the exchange rate needs to be raised, the central bank increases
its demand for US $ in the foreign exchange market. Other things remaining constant, higher
demand for US $ would raise the price of US $, as desired. This would lead to depreciation of
the domestic currency.
Briefly, managed floating is an exercise of sale and purchase of foreign currency by the central bank,
so that the exchange rate is managed within the desired limits.
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
• Managed floating is a tool employed by the central bank to restore the value of the country's currency
(in relation to other currencies) within the desired limits, even when exchange rate is determined by the
market forces of demand and supply.
• In fact, managed floating may be called as the mixture of both flexible and fixed exchange rate systems.
- It comprises the element of flexible exchange rate system as the exchange rate is primarily determined
by the forces of supply and demand.
- Likewise, it comprises the element of fixed exchange rate system as the exchange rate is moderated
(or managed) by way of intervention by the RBI.

(5) Grants and Donations: Grants and donations (unilateral payments) to rest of the world also

(6) Payment of Incomes: Demand for foreign exchange in the domestic economy also arises

is held/demanded by the people for purpose of speculative trading. Often, more foreign
exchange is held when the exchange rate is low, and vice versa.

Functions
Foreign exchange market performs the following functions:
(1) Transfer Function: It implies transfer of purchasing power in terms of foreign exchange
across different countries of the world.
(2) Credit Function: It implies provision of credit in terms of foreign exchange for the export and
import of goods and services across different countries of world.
(3) Hedging Function: It implies protection against risk related to variations in foreign exchange
rate. Exchange rate is locked for future supplies of foreign exchange.
Operation of Foreign Exchange Market
Foreign exchange market operates either as
• Spot Market (Current Market), or as
• Forward Market.
Following is a brief description of both these types:
Spot Market (Current Market)
Spot market for foreign exchange is that market which handles only spot transactions or current
transactions.
Its principal characteristics are that:
(i) In terms of 'period of transaction', spot market is of 'daily nature". It does not trade in future
deliveries.
(ii) The rate of exchange which is determined in the spot market is known as spot rate of
exchange. The spot rate of exchange (or current rate of exchange) is that rate which prevails
at the time when transactions are made.
Forward Market
Forward market for foreign exchange is that market which handles such transactions of foreign
exchange that are meant for future delivery. Such transactions are signed today but are to materialise
(or are to be honoured) on some future date.
Principal characteristics of forward market are that:
(i) It only caters to forward transactions; it does not deal with spot transactions in foreign
exchange.
(ii) It defines (or determines) forward exchange rate-the exchange rate at which forward
transactions are to be honoured.
543

Introductory Macroeconomics
Why are Forward Transactions Contracted?
Forward transactions are contracted for two reasons:
(i) To avoid the risk of any adverse change in exchange rate, and
(i) To make speculative gains.

boxes.text:
Revaluation of the Currency is different from Appreciation of the currency
The difference is as under:
• Appreciation of the (domestic) currency occurs when the value of the (domestic) curency rises in
the international money market, because of the market forces of supply and demand. The government
plays no role whatsoever.
• Revaluation of the (domestic) currency occurs when the value of the domestic currency is deliberately
raised by the government by lowering the exchange rate. The market forces of supply and demand play
no role whatsoever.
Less Developed Countries often Devalue their Currency
Less developed countries often devalue their currency: domestic currency is made cheaper in relation to
the foreign currency. This is because of the three principal reasons:
) Devaluation (implying a planned fall in the value of the domestic currency) is expected to raise the
demand for the domestically produced goods and services. Accordingly, exports are expected
to rise.
(i) Rise in exports (owing to devaluation) is expected to increase the supply of foreign exchange
into the domestic economy. This facilitates import of essential goods from rest of the world.
(i) A fall in the value of domestic currency induces private foreign investment. Because, for every
dollar, the investors are going to get more rupees, after devaluation. This is expected to promote
GDP growth.
Gold Standard System of Exchange Rate -
An Old Variant of Fixed Exchange Rate System
• Gold standard system of exchange rate is an old variant of fixed exchange rate system.
• According to this system (prevalent in most countries prior to 1920s), gold was taken as the
common unit of parity between currencies of different countries. Each country was to define
value of its currency in terms of gold. Accordingly, value of one currency in terms of the other
currency was fixed considering gold value of each currency.
Example:
If UK € (Pound) = 4 g of gold, and US $ (Dollar) = 2 g of gold, then 1 UKE = 2 USS.
Exchange rate or exchange ratio between UK E and US $ = 1: 2. Two US dollars would
exchange for 1 UK pound.
• This system of exchange was also known as Mint Par Value of Exchange or Mint Parity. Mint value
of a currency implied gold value of that currency.
Bretton Woods System of Exchange Rate
Adjustable Peg System of Exchange Rate
Bretton Woods System (even when it was a fixed system of exchange rate) allowed some adjustments.
So, it was called 'adjustable peg system of exchange rate'. According to this system,
Different currencies were pegged (or related) to one currency, that is US dollar. US dollar was
ed gold value at a fixed price.

11.4.2 (a) Flexible Exchange Rate System: Merits
A shift from fixed exchange rate system to flexible exchange rate system was desired in view of its
merits. Some of the principal merits of flexible exchange rate system (in relation to fixed exchange
rate system) are as under:
(1) Large Reserves of Forex not required: Flexible system of exchange rate does not require
large reserves of foreign exchange with the government. Market forces of supply and
demand automatically drive the rate of exchange to the point of equilibrium.
(2) Efficient Allocation of Resources: Flexible exchange rate system leads to equilibrium
exchange rates of different currencies. Accordingly, allocation of resources (across different
countries of the world) is expected to become more and more efficient/optimum.
(3) Large Size of the Forex Market: Since foreign exchange itself becomes a trading commodity.
the size of forex market tends to be large. This induces economic growth across all parts of
the world.
(4) International Mobility of Liquidity: Since large reserves of forex are not required, flexible
exchange rate tends to promote international mobility of liquidity. This is good for the less.
developed countries (like India), where foreign investment is a significant determinant of
GDP growth.

exchange rate system are as under:
(1) Marginalisation of Weak Currencies: Flexible exchange rate system leads to marginalisation
of weak currencies in the international money market. Owing to their low demand, weak
currencies (of small economies) often suffer huge depreciation in relation to strong currencies (of
big economies).

(i) Repayment of international loans, (i) Investment in rest of the world, (ill) Imports, (iv) Direct
purchases abroad, (v) Grants and donations, (vi) Payment of incomes, and (vil) Speculative
trading.
• Supply of Foreign Currency/Foreign Exchange depends upon:
(il) Investments from rest of the world
(i) Exports
(ili) Direct purchases by rest of the world
(iv) Loans from rest of the world
(v) Grants and donations from rest of the world (vi) Income receipts
(vii) Remittances by the non-residents
• Foreign Exchange Market refers to the market for national currencies of different countries of the
world.
• Functions: (i) Transfer function, (i) Credit function, and (il) Hedging function.
• Spot Market deals with current sale and purchase of foreign exchange. It determines spot rate of
exchange.
Forward Market deals with such sale and purchase of foreign exchange which are contracted
today but are implemented sometimes in the future. It determines forward rate of exchange.

title: Balance of Payments
intro: Balance of payments is a statement of accounts showing all monetary transactions of a country with the rest of the world during a period of time, generally one year.

lessons.title: Balance of payments: account and recording rule
lessons.body: Balance of payments is a statement of accounts showing all monetary transactions of a country with the rest of the world during a period of time, generally one year. It records goods, services, income, transfers and asset-related transactions between residents and non-residents. Foreign-exchange receipts are credit items; payments are debit items. The textbook uses current, capital and official-reserves accounts. Keep its school-level account terminology when answering.

lessons.title: Current account, trade balance and invisibles
lessons.body: Current account records exports and imports of goods and services, factor income and current transfers. Goods are visible trade or merchandise; services, factor incomes and transfers are invisibles. Balance of trade covers goods only. A gift from abroad is a current transfer; wages for a service are factor income. The supplied purple box treats direct tourist purchases as invisible trade: preserve that convention for this textbook.
lessons.formula:
Trade balance = Goods exports − Goods imports
Current-account balance = Trade balance + Net services + Net factor income + Net current transfers

lessons.title: Capital account and asset/liability changes
lessons.body: Capital account records transactions that change a country’s assets or liabilities in relation to the rest of the world. The textbook includes borrowing, foreign investment, NRI deposits, banking capital and short-term debt. Inward FDI or an external loan is a credit; an outward investment or repayment of foreign loan principal is a debit. Interest on a foreign loan belongs in the current account; the principal belongs in the capital account. FDI involves a lasting productive interest/control; portfolio investment purchases financial securities.

lessons.title: Official reserves, deficit and surplus
lessons.body: If autonomous foreign-exchange payments exceed autonomous receipts, there is a BoP deficit, financed by accommodating transactions such as a drawdown of reserves or official borrowing. A surplus can increase official reserves. A decrease in reserve assets finances a shortfall; an increase uses foreign exchange. Follow the sign convention explicitly stated in a numerical instead of confusing a positive stock increase with a credit entry.

lessons.title: Autonomous versus accommodating transactions
lessons.body: Autonomous transactions are undertaken for independent economic motives such as profit, rather than to correct a BoP imbalance; they are above-the-line items. Accommodating transactions are undertaken to finance or correct the imbalance and are below the line. A foreign loan may be autonomous when raised commercially or accommodating when arranged specifically to finance a deficit. Classification depends on purpose, not merely the type of transaction.
lessons.textbookHeading: 12.3.1 Autonomous and Accommodating Items of BoP Account

lessons.title: Accounting balance versus operational balance
lessons.body: BoP balances in the accounting sense because every transaction has a counterpart and financing entries close the accounts. This does not mean autonomous receipts equal autonomous payments or that the economy has no external problem. A current-account deficit financed by foreign borrowing is consistent with accounting balance and increasing indebtedness. Read the Ability Zone worked table to see a current-account deficit offset by capital inflows.
lessons.textbookHeading: ABILITY ZONE · Balance of Payments: Accounting Sense and Operational Sense

lessons.title: Causes and significance of disequilibrium
lessons.body: Economic causes include large development imports, business cycles, domestic inflation, import substitution and changes in trading partners’ costs. Political instability can discourage foreign investment; policy changes can increase imports. Social causes include changes in tastes and cross-border preferences. BoP data show external strengths, weaknesses, debt and reserve pressures and help formulate policy. A trade deficit alone does not tell you the whole BoP position.

Introductory Macroeconomics
12.1 BoP (or BoP ACCOUNTS)
Meaning and Concept of BoP
Balance of payments (BoP) is a statement of accounts showing all monetary transactions of a
country with the rest of the world during a period of time, generally one year. Being monetary
transactions, these are also called economic transactions. These transactions may be made by the
individuals, firms and the government of a country. Broadly, the monetary transactions relate to:
i) export (X) and import (M) of goods. In the BoP language, it is called 'merchandise' or
'visible trade' (simply because goods are visible when they cross the borders or goods can
be seen),
(ii) export and import of services. It is called 'invisible trade' (simply because services are not
visible when they cross the borders or services cannot be seen),
(iii) international sale and purchase of financial assets. Financial assets include stocks and
bonds, and
(iv) international sale and purchase of real assets. Real assets are like plant and machinery.
•There is an inflow of foreign exchange into the country when we export goods and services or
when the foreigners invest in our financial or real assets. Likewise, there is an outflow of foreign
exchange from our country to rest of the world when we import goods and services or when our
residents invest in the financial or real assets of other countries.
BoP accounts record all receipts and payments of foreign exchange. Receipts are recorded as
credit items, while payments are recorded as debit items. The BoP accounts, thus prepared, reflect
performance of our economy in relation to rest of the world.
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Non-inclusion of Tourist Spending on Goods as 'Export' or 'Import'
• Only such goods are treated as 'export or 'import which are tangible and can be seen crossing the
borders as merchandise.
• Goods bought by the foreign tourists in the domestic markets are not treated as 'export.
Likewise goods purchased by the domestic tourists in rest of the world are not treated as import.
• All direct purchases by non-resident tourists in the domestic economy and by resident tourists abroad
are treated as "invisible trade.
12.2 COMPONENTS OF BoP ACCOUNT
BoP accounts include the following components:
Components of BoP Accounts
Current Account
Capital Account
Official Reserves Account
566
Balance of Payments
Following is their brief description:
12.2.1 Current Account
Meaning and Concept of Current Account
Current account records receipt and payment of foreign exchange on account of such transactions
which do not impact asset-liability status of a country in relation to rest of the world. Liabilities or
assets of a country (in relation to rest of the world) are neither raised nor reduced. In other words,
current account transactions do not give rise to 'future claims.
Components of Current Account
Principal components (items) of current account BoP are as under:
(1) Export and Import of Goods: Export and import of goods is treated as 'merchandise or
'visible trade'. This is a visible trade because goods are tangible (material) and therefore, can
be seen while crossing the borders.
Example:
Export or import of smart-phones can be seen while crossing the borders.
(2) Export and Import of Services: Export and import of services is treated as invisible trade!. This is
because services are not tangible (material) and therefore, cannot be seen while crossing the
borders.
Example:
Insurance services being rendered across the borders cannot be seen as crossing the
borders.
Services are further classified as: factor services and non-factor services.
(i) Factor Services: Factor services are those which lead to factor payments or factor
income.
> In the BoP accounts, monetary transactions related to factor incomes are split as:
(a) investment income, and (b) compensation of employees.
> Investment income includes income on account of rent, interest and profit.
In BoP Accounts:
Factor Incomes = Compensation of employees
+ Investment income (= rent + interest + profit)
(ii) Non-factor Services: Non-factor services include all services, other than factor services.
Insurance and banking services may be cited as examples.
> Monetary transactions related to non-factor services are recorded as receipts when
these services are exported, and as payments when these services are imported.
(3) Current Transfers: Current transfers refer to transfers for free. These are unilateral transfers
made by way of gifts, grants and remittances (by the residents settled abroad), In the Bop
accounts, current transfers are treated as an element of 'invisibles".

Q. 1. State whether the following items are visible or invisible items of trade:
(i) Export of laptops to Nepal
(il) Insurance services to Bhutan
(il) Export of coffee from Coorg
(iv) Import of COVID vaccines from USA
(v) Consultancy services of KPMG India used by a foreign firm
Ans. Visible Items: (i), (iii, (iv)
Invisible Items: (ii), (v)
Q. 2. In what way do current account transactions not lead to future claims?
Ans. Current account transactions (such as trade in goods and services and current transfers) do not
lead to future claims in the sense that these transactions (unlike capital account transactions like
borrowings) do not lead to any contractual obligation to be settled in future.
Q. 3. How is the import of services recorded in the BoP, and what does it signify?
Ans. The import of services is recorded as a debit item in the current account of BoP, and is recorded
as invisible trade. It signifies outflow of foreign exchange to rest of the world impacting
CAD (current account balance)
CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Important Observations
• In the BoP accounts, current transfers are treated as an element of invisibles. So that, invisibles in
the BoP accounts include:
(i) monetary transactions related to export and import of factor services,
(i) monetary transactions related to export and import of non-factor services, and
(i) monetary transactions related to current transfers.

CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Q. 4. Name three such items which are not included in balance of trade.
Ans. Three items which are not included in balance of trade are:
(i) Export and import of services such as of shipping, insurance and banking.
(ii) Interest and dividend payments between the countries.
(iii) Expenditure by the tourists.
Q. 5. What is the difference between balance of trade and current account balance?
Ans. Balance of trade refers to the balance occurring on account of export and import of visible items
(goods only).
Current account balance includes the balance of trade as well as balance on invisibles.
12.2.2 Capital Account
Meaning and Concept of Capital Account
• Capital account records receipts and payments of such transactions which cause an impact on
asset-liability status of a country in relation to rest of the world. Liabilities or assets of a country
(in relation to rest of the world) are either raised or reduced. In other words, capital account
transactions lead to future claims.
Confusion is sometimes raised with regard to the export and import of capital goods, like plant
and machinery. Should such transactions be included in the capital account?
• Answer is 'No'. Let it be absolutely clear that the export and import of all types of goods (consumer
goods or capital goods) is recorded as 'merchandise' or 'visible trade' in the current account of
BoP. Thus, export and import of capital goods has nothing to do with capital account of BoP.
DID YOU KNOW
• Export and import of capital goods (plant and machinery) is NOT included in the capital account.
• Export and import of all types of goods (consumer goods or capital goods) is recorded as
'merchandise' or 'visible trade' in the current account of BoP.
Components of Capital Account
Two principal components of capital account are:
(1) Borrowing: Borrowing is split as:
(i) External Commercial Borrowing: It is available at the market rate of interest (in the
international money market).
(ii) External Assistance: It is available at the concessional rate of interest.
> Borrowing from rest of the world raises our liability to rest of the world. But, note it
carefully, that it is recorded as a 'credit item" in the capital account of BoP. The reason
is this: all receipts of foreign exchange are recorded as credit items in the BoP accounts.
> Thus, borrowing of rest of the world (or lending to rest of the world) would be
recorded as 'debit item' in the capital account, as it causes flow of foreign exchange
from our country to rest of the world.
(2) Foreign Investment: Foreign investment is split as:
(i) Portfolio Investment: It basically refers to foreign institutional investment (FIl). It is
investment by rest of the world in shares and bonds of the domestic companies.
571
570

Introductory Macroeconomics
(ii) Foreign Direct investment: It relates to ownership of enterprises in the domestic
economy by rest of the world.
Example:
Walmart stores in India.
Other Components of Capital Account
Besides, borrowing and investment (which are the principal components or capital account) there are
other components, as under:
(3) NRI Deposits: In the context of the Indian economy, deposits is also a significant
constituent of capital account. However, here a note of caution is essential:
• Only such NRI deposits are to be considered (as a component of capital account) which are
made in the domestic economy. Thus, non resident Indians should make deposits in India,
• It also needs to be noted that money sent by the NRIs to their families in India is to be
treated as current transfers", and are to be recorded in current account of Bop. Only
deposits held by NRIs in the domestic economy are to be considered as a component of
capital account.
(4) Banking Capital (Other than NRI Deposits): Banking capital is yet another component of
capital account. Banking Capital refers to 'foreign assets' held by the commercial banks.
• Owing to drawdown of foreign assets of the commercial banks (the commercial banks
converting their foreign assets into liquidity, inflow of foreign exchange into the domestic
economy tends to rise.
(5) Short-term Trade Credit: In the context of the Indian BoP, short-term trade credit is another
important component of capital account. It arises on account of purchases in the international
market without making immediate payment.
• Repayment of short-term debt to rest of the world leads to outflow of foreign exchange to
rest of the world. Accordingly, it is recorded in the capital account with a negative sign.
Inward flow of foreign exchange (from rest of the world), on the other hand, is recorded
with a positive sign.

CRITICAL TERMS & CONCEPTS
Change in Official Reserves in BoP Accounting
In the Balance of Payments (BoP) system, the total inflows (credits) and outflows (debits) must balance
to zero. The change in official reserves is crucial in maintaining this balance.
(i) '+' sign = Decrease in official reserves (inflow of foreign currency).
(ii) - sign = Increase in official reserves (outflow of domestic currency).
These signs reflect whether a country is increasing or decreasing its stock of reserves.
(i) Increase in Official Reserves (-sign): An increase in reserves, such as purchasing foreign currency,
represents an outflow of domestic currency. This represents a debit in the BoP, as it reflects a use of
domestic financial resources. In the context of the BoP, an outflow of resources (like buying foreign
reserves) is a debit, and debits are traditionally represented with a minus sign.

(il) Decrease in Official Reserves (+ sign): A decrease in reserves, such as selling foreign assets,
reflects an inflow of foreign currency, Selling foreign reserves or reducing them increases the supply
of domestic currency in the economy (as the central bank might buy back domestic currency i
exchange for foreign currency, and this is considered a credit in the Bor accounting system
12.3 EQUILIBRIUM AND DISEQUILIBRIUM IN BOP
Equilibrium in BoP
• BoP equilibrium is struck when: Current account balance + Capital account balance + errors and
omissions = Zero, and there is no movement (increase or decrease) of official reserves of the
central bank. In case we ignore the element of errors and omissions, we can st
equilibrium is stuck when:
Current account balance + Capital account balance = Zero
and there is no movement (increase/decrease) of the official reserves.
• We can say that BoP is in a state of equilibrium when any negative balance in the current account
is equally counterbalanced by a positive balance in the capital account, and there is no changein
official reserves of the central bank.
• Thus, in a state of BoP equilibrium inward flow of foreign exchange (on account of current account
and capital account transactions) is exactly equal to the outward flow of foreign exchange, and
there is no change in official reserves (of foreign exchange and gold) with the central bank of the
country.
Disequilibrium in BoP
• Disequilibrium in BoP occurs when the sum total of current account balance and capital account
balance is not zero; instead it is either some positive number or some negative number.
• In case the sum total of current account balance and capital account balance is some posive
number, it indicates BoP Surplus. On the other hand, if the sum total of current account balance
and capital account balance is some negative number, it indicates BoP Deficit.
Thus, we have:
(1) BoP Disequilibrium when: Current account balance + Capital account balance is NOT equal
to zero, and it causes the movement of official reserves.
(ii) BoP Surplus when: Current account balance + Capital account balance is some posi

12.3.1 Autonomous and Accommodating Items of BoP Account
• BoP transactions or items in BoP account are often classified as autonomous items and
accommodating items. The difference is as under:
• Autonomous items refer to such BoP transactions which are undertaken with a view to making
profits. It is due to these transactions that there is a BoP deficit/surplus.
• Accommodating items, on the other hand, refer to such transactions which are undertaken by the
central bank of a country with a view to correcting BoP imbalance and restoring BoP equilibrium.
• It is important to note that accommodating items do not cause any movement of goods and
services across the borders. These relate only to the movement of official reserves with a view to
correcting BoP imbalances.
• Often the accommodating items are not reflected as an element of BoP accounts. These are
therefore called 'below the line' items, while autonomous items are called 'above the line' items.
Thus, when BoP deficit/surplus is estimated, it is with reference to only the autonomous items or
autonomous transactions of BoP.

Having understood the concept and composition of BoP accounts, we can now write the significance

policies. In the event of greater flow of foreign exchange from rest of the world, there is a
pressure of demand for the domestic currency.

Power Points [Summary of the Chapter]
• Balance of Payments is a summary statement of all monetary (or economic) transactions between a
country and rest of the world.
• Components:
• Current account
• Capital account
• Official reserves account.
• Economic Transactions in BoP are broadly classified as:
• merchandise
• invisibles
• transactions leading to change in the ownership of assets vis-a-vis rest of the world.
• Components:
- Export and import of goods
• Export and import of services [(a) factor services + (b) non-factor services]
• Current transfers.
• Export and import of goods is called 'merchandise' or 'visible trade'.
• Invisibles include: Non-factor services, Factor income, Current transfers
• Balance of Trade (or Trade Balance) = Export of merchandise - Import of merchandise
• Current Account Balance = Trade balance + Invisibles balance.
• Capital Account records receipts and payments of foreign exchange of a country on account of such
transactions which impact asset-liability status of a country in relation to rest of the world.
• Components:
› Borrowing
> Foreign investment
> NRI deposits
> Banking capital
> Short-term debt.
• Borrowing includes: external commercial borrowing, and external assistance.
• Investment includes: FIl (Foreign Institutional Investment), and FDI (Foreign Direct Investment).
• Capital Account Balance shows net capital flows.
• Positive Balance shows that inward flow of capital is greater than the outward flow.
• Negative Balance shows that inward flow of capital is less than the outward flow.
• BoP Equilibrium is a situation when current account balance and capital account balance add up to
zero, and there is no movement (increase or decrease) in official reserves.
Or, it is a situation when receipts and payments of a country on account of economic transactions
with rest of the world are exactly equal to each other, and there is no movement of official reserves.
• BoP Deficit occurs when payments of a country on account of economic transactions with rest of
the world exceed its receipts and consequently, there is a decrease in official reserves.
• BoP Surplus occurs when receipts of a country on account of economic transactions with rest of
the world exceed its payments and consequently, there is increase in official reserves.
• Autonomous Items refer to such BoP transactions which are determined by considerations of profit.
It is due to these transactions that the BoP deficit/surplus arises. These are called 'above the line
items.
• Accommodating Items refer to such BoP transactions which are not determined by considerations of
profit. It is due to these transactions that the BoP deficit/surplus is corrected. These are called below
the line items.

12.2.2 Capital Account
Meaning and Concept of Capital Account
• Capital account records receipts and payments of such transactions which cause an impact on
asset-liability status of a country in relation to rest of the world. Liabilities or assets of a country
(in relation to rest of the world) are either raised or reduced. In other words, capital account
transactions lead to future claims.
Confusion is sometimes raised with regard to the export and import of capital goods, like plant
and machinery. Should such transactions be included in the capital account?
• Answer is 'No'. Let it be absolutely clear that the export and import of all types of goods (consumer
goods or capital goods) is recorded as 'merchandise' or 'visible trade' in the current account of
BoP. Thus, export and import of capital goods has nothing to do with capital account of BoP.
DID YOU KNOW
• Export and import of capital goods (plant and machinery) is NOT included in the capital account.
• Export and import of all types of goods (consumer goods or capital goods) is recorded as
'merchandise' or 'visible trade' in the current account of BoP.
Components of Capital Account
Two principal components of capital account are:
(1) Borrowing: Borrowing is split as:
(i) External Commercial Borrowing: It is available at the market rate of interest (in the
international money market).
(ii) External Assistance: It is available at the concessional rate of interest.
> Borrowing from rest of the world raises our liability to rest of the world. But, note it
carefully, that it is recorded as a 'credit item" in the capital account of BoP. The reason
is this: all receipts of foreign exchange are recorded as credit items in the BoP accounts.
> Thus, borrowing of rest of the world (or lending to rest of the world) would be
recorded as 'debit item' in the capital account, as it causes flow of foreign exchange
from our country to rest of the world.
(2) Foreign Investment: Foreign investment is split as:
(i) Portfolio Investment: It basically refers to foreign institutional investment (FIl). It is
investment by rest of the world in shares and bonds of the domestic companies.

boxes.text:
Change in Official Reserves in BoP Accounting
In the Balance of Payments (BoP) system, the total inflows (credits) and outflows (debits) must balance
to zero. The change in official reserves is crucial in maintaining this balance.
(i) '+' sign = Decrease in official reserves (inflow of foreign currency).
(ii) - sign = Increase in official reserves (outflow of domestic currency).
These signs reflect whether a country is increasing or decreasing its stock of reserves.
(i) Increase in Official Reserves (-sign): An increase in reserves, such as purchasing foreign currency,
represents an outflow of domestic currency. This represents a debit in the BoP, as it reflects a use of
domestic financial resources. In the context of the BoP, an outflow of resources (like buying foreign
reserves) is a debit, and debits are traditionally represented with a minus sign.

• Negative Balance shows that inward flow of capital is less than the outward flow.
• BoP Equilibrium is a situation when current account balance and capital account balance add up to
zero, and there is no movement (increase or decrease) in official reserves.
Or, it is a situation when receipts and payments of a country on account of economic transactions
with rest of the world are exactly equal to each other, and there is no movement of official reserves.
• BoP Deficit occurs when payments of a country on account of economic transactions with rest of
the world exceed its receipts and consequently, there is a decrease in official reserves.
• BoP Surplus occurs when receipts of a country on account of economic transactions with rest of
the world exceed its payments and consequently, there is increase in official reserves.
• Autonomous Items refer to such BoP transactions which are determined by considerations of profit.
It is due to these transactions that the BoP deficit/surplus arises. These are called 'above the line
items.
• Accommodating Items refer to such BoP transactions which are not determined by considerations of
profit. It is due to these transactions that the BoP deficit/surplus is corrected. These are called below
the line items.
